news.title: California Dems’ doomed ICE stunt rightfully shredded by judge
news.text:
California’s latest attempt to override the US Constitution in service of a radical left-wing agenda has just been thrown out by the federal courts.

This week, United States District Judge Christina A. Snyder issued a permanent injunction barring the state from enforcing two laws (SB 627 and 805) that would require Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to wear badges, and prevent them from wearing masks.

It is beyond obvious why ICE agents need those protections. The far left and its street militias will stop at nothing to stalk, harass, and attack anyone who works for ICE. Exposing the personal information of any ICE agent would put him or her in grave danger, and undermine the rule of law.

Democrats in Sacramento (notably Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, who introduced both laws) simply ignored these risks, and voted to put the men and women who protect our country in danger.

It was clear from the beginning that these laws were unconstitutional. They carved out an exception for the California Highway Patrol, which is unlawful discrimination against federal officers. Wiener introduced a new law (SB 1004) that purported to address that problem, but which still suffered from the fatal flaw of encroaching on immigration enforcement, which is an area of exclusive federal jurisdiction.

Democrats cannot have it both ways. They cannot demand that states like Arizona have no power to enforce federal immigration law, while also trying to use their supermajority in the California Legislature to direct ICE agents in their jobs.

California Democrats have a habit of passing laws that are unconstitutional on their face, simply to generate partisan propaganda and friendly media coverage. 

Perhaps the most ridiculous example came in 2024, when Gavin Newsom tried to ban the use of “deepfake” AI videos making fun of politicians like Kamala Harris. The federal judiciary tossed that law out at the earliest opportunity as a violation of the First Amendment. Today, Democrats freely use AI-generated videos for political purposes, and nobody seems bothered by it.

It is a disgrace that California and other Democrat-run states still refuse to allow federal officers to enforce bipartisan immigration law. They are following the poisonous precedent of the South in the era of slavery, when states claimed the power to nullify federal law. 

Like the Confederate heresy, Democrats’ perverse “sanctuary” philosophy will be judged by history for the grave affront to democracy that it really is.
news.summary: California’s latest attempt to override the US Constitution in service of a radical left-wing agenda has just been thrown out by the federal courts.

news.title: Ahead of 2028, a presidential campaign is building behind AOC
news.text:
At the height of midterm hustings, Donald Trump made a peculiar comment about one of his fiercest critics in Congress.

"Somehow I don't mind AOC that much," the US president said at a Michigan rally, using Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's nickname. "I don't know why, she doesn't bug me too much."

It could have been a sign the dial has shifted on the Democratic representative, from firebrand progressive to an unlikely bridge between America's far left and the right.

And in the wake of the midterms' "bluenami", speculation that Ms Ocasio-Cortez is popular enough to be elected president has reached a fever pitch.

Almost a dozen Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) chapters, including in Chicago, Los Angeles, San Diego and Washington DC, have recently passed resolutions urging her to launch a 2028 campaign.

Separately, a political organisation called Ready for AOC launched earlier this month, aiming to gather at least a million signatures in support of a presidential run.

There are suggestions Ms Ocasio-Cortez would be a serious contender outside socialist ranks as well.

Just days before the midterms, an AtlasIntel poll asked blue voters who they would support in the party primaries for the 2028 election.

Ms Ocasio-Cortez ranked second, only a slim margin behind Georgia senator Jon Ossoff and 5 points higher than the party's last presidential candidate, Kamala Harris.

On Kalshi and Polymarket, America's two best-known betting markets - according to US political media outlet The Hill - she similarly has the second-highest odds next to Mr Ossoff.

From bartender to potential president

From the moment Ms Ocasio-Cortez entered politics — when she pulled off the biggest primary upset in 2018 to beat 10-term incumbent and Democratic Caucus chair Joe Crowley — there has been talk of her presidential potential.

At 29, the former bartender became the youngest woman and youngest Latina ever elected to Congress.

Only months later, an NBC News poll found three-quarters of Democratic and leaning-blue voters would consider voting for her to be president.

In the years since, she has become one of America's most followed politicians online, where her socialist-leaning policies of Medicare for all, stronger immigrant rights and affordable housing have drawn an audience of millions.

Ms Ocasio-Cortez has not yet said whether she will run for president in 2028, but her office released a memo touting her wide appeal after the Democrats' resounding midterms victory on November 3.

"Rep. Ocasio-Cortez has built a record of success that extends beyond her own electoral victories … [emerging] as one of the most powerful endorsements in the United States and New York State specifically," it read.

One of the achievements listed was her "race-changing endorsement" of fellow Democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani, who comfortably won the New York City mayoral race last year on promises of free childcare, free city buses and freezing rents.

It also highlighted how she held three major rallies and raised $US1 million ($1.48 million) in support for Abdul El-Sayed, whose victory in Michigan was one of the party's major midterm successes.

But the memo began with Ms Ocasio-Cortez's reflections after the 2024 presidential election when support for Mr Trump surged in her district of the Bronx.

Many of Ms Ocasio-Cortez's supporters split their tickets to vote for both her and Mr Trump, whose numbers in the largely Black, Asian and Latino district jumped 11 per cent.

At the same time, Ms Ocasio-Cortez was comfortably re-elected to a fourth term, securing almost 69 per cent of votes in the House race.

"There is universal frustration in this country, much of it I think justified, that is raging at a political establishment that centres corporate interests and billionaires and puts their needs ahead of the needs of working Americans," she said at the time, after reaching out to those voters.

AOC's reach over party divides

In the two years since, she has worked to position herself as a champion of the working class and a "kind of friendly neighbourhood lefty", according to The New York Times's Matt Flegenheimer, who said she evoked both "the people-over-profits populism of Bernie Sanders and the more-unites-than-divides-us appeals of Barack Obama".

As part of her evolution, Ms Ocasio-Cortez has met with Make America Healthy Again activists, where she has found common ground on issues like pesticides, and people in rural Georgia whose homes are now beside a massive Meta data centre.

In her comments about a potential presidential run, Ms Ocasio-Cortez has not shied away from the roadblocks in her path.

At the top of that list is the fact the United States has never elected a woman as president. Across Congress, men outnumber women almost three to one.

"Pretty candidly, I think about my identity," Ms Ocasio-Cortez told The New York Times in September.

In the same interview, Ms Ocasio-Cortez said some people had suggested 2028 may be her "political window".

"Oftentimes in politics, you do only get one shot … life doesn't wait for you to be ready for things. Sometimes life just makes things ready for you," she said.

Is the US ready for a progressive president?

The speculation comes as the Democratic Party turns to internal battles, with some cautioning against leaning too far left and others seeing the midterm results as an endorsement of progressive policies.

There are also suggestions Ms Ocasio-Cortez will run for the Senate instead, as New York Democrat Chuck Schumer is up for re-election in 2028 and has not yet said whether he plans to run.

Doug Sosnik, a senior advisor to former president Bill Clinton, described Ms Ocasio-Cortez as an "unbelievable political talent" who has "the Zeitgeist of our times" at her fingertips.

But he questioned whether her appeal could extend beyond the Democratic base.

"I think she would be an extremely powerful force in the Democratic primary," Mr Sosnik told AP.

Others, including in Republican circles, have taken a more positive view.

Andrew Kolvet, executive producer of The Charlie Kirk Show and a spokesperson for Turning Point USA, said Ms Ocasio-Cortez was seen as "a Democrat with game".

"AOC and Mamdani, yes, they have awful policies and ideas, but they are inarguably the best raw political talents of the far left," he said.

DSA spokesperson Cara Tobe said the Democrats' overwhelming success at the midterms "would not have been possible without a socialist surge".

"People are starting to realise and learn that socialism is not a big scary word," she told AP.

"The big thing is people are looking for change. This is actually part of what even led Trump to victory."
news.summary: In the wake of the midterms' "bluenami", speculation that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is popular enough to be elected America's first female president has reached a fever pitch.
news.author: Annabel Bowles

news.title: 'The View' co-host stunned as Hostin backs Gavin Newsom bypassing victims' families for death row commutations
news.text: "The View" co-host Ana Navarro appeared surprised when co-host Sunny Hostin disagreed with her argument that Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom should have notified the victims' families before ending the death sentences of 548 inmates in his state. "I don’t like the way it went through. And I think that before he announced that, he needed to get the approval and agreement of the families of the victims, because the people that he’s commuted the sentences for are people who are on death row. They’re people who committed murder, and I tend to be against blanket pardon to begin with," Navarro said. Newsom commuted the death sentences of all of California's death-row inmates in early November, effectively ending capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions. CALIFORNIA PROSECUTORS SLAM NEWSOM'S DEATH ROW COMMUTATIONS, ACCUSE GOVERNOR OF PUTTING 'POLITICS OVER PEOPLE' "I think these are things you have to take on a case-by-case basis, and I think it’s disrespectful to the victims’ families," Navarro said. "You can disagree or agree with the death penalty, but to me, if your loved one has been murdered, you have the right to be told that this is happening, before you read about it." Hostin said, "I disagree with that." "That the victim's family should have been told?" Navarro asked in response. "Yes," Hostin repeated. "I'm an opponent of the death penalty. I think that God gives life." Hostin said those cases were under Newsom's purview as governor. She argued that the system is "broken," and no one should have to pay the ultimate price for a broken system. ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION "One innocent person being put to death is not worth the entire system," she said. "And if you look at the system, it's not a deterrent. That the statistics show that more than half of death row exonerees are Black, even though Black people just make up 13.6% of the U.S. population. "And nearly 60% of the people that are found to have been wrongfully convicted of murder by the Innocence Project are African Americans, and so the system is broken," Hostin continued. "And you should not pay the ultimate price for a system that is broken." Co-host Alyssa Farah Griffin sided with Navarro, arguing the move was a betrayal of the families. "It was a betrayal of the families to not notify them beforehand," Griffin said. "People can agree or disagree on the death penalty. It's actually come up as a ballot initiative in California twice in the last decade. And California voters actually voted to keep capital punishment in place. "I think (Newsom) has the purview to do this, but then to not notify families, that gets in the way of their grief," she added. "There's no greater trauma than having a loved one murdered in a brutal way and thinking it's been adjudicated in the court, and there's a certain outcome in finding out in a newspaper, basically, that that's not happening." GAVIN NEWSOM SEEKS COUNSEL FROM ‘MASTER’ BILL CLINTON AS HE PLOTS PROJECT 2029 Griffin also said it could be a political move by Newsom. "This should have been handled better," she said. "And I think there's a political side to this too. He wants to run for president. He wants to seem more progressive. Kamala Harris may run for president. He's gonna be like, ‘She was a prosecutor who put people in jail.’ So, I don't like it. He should have notified the families." Co-host Sara Haines agreed, arguing that undoing all the death sentences treated each case the same. "I think the point is that if you want to change something going forward, put it on a ballot, and clearly California doesn't want it taken off," she said. "At that point, I think he should have looked case-by-case, because to not reach out to these families, they get nothing back. "Any closure they get is small. But some of these people deeply found something in this conviction and this determination. And to just undo it in one blanket swipe is to treat them all the same." When reached for comment, the governor's office referred Fox News Digital to a letter Newsom issued explaining his decision. In part, Newsom wrote, "This decision is among the most difficult of my career, not because I doubt its necessity for our state but because I know its announcement may surface excruciating memories for victims' families. I deeply respect the views of those who will strongly disagree with my decision, including some families of victims who have suffered the worst possible loss. "I hold this painful truth along with the belief that this is a righteous action," he continued. "Today I am acting on my long and deeply held conviction that individually and collectively we are stronger as a society when we reject state-sanctioned killing." Later in the letter, Newsom said, "California voters have voted to keep the death penalty on the books, and I respect that. I recognize the limits of this clemency action, which does not repeal the death penalty and is limited to commuting California's current death sentences. The power to repeal the death penalty rests with the Legislature and voters." CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "Victims’ rights were disregarded and trampled by Governor Newsom," Y. David Scharf, chairman of Morrison Cohen LLP, told Fox News Digital in a statement. "Whatever one’s view of the death penalty, the families of murder victims deserved more than to learn that the sentences in their loved ones’ cases were being swept away as part of a blanket decision affecting hundreds of cases. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The governor may have the constitutional authority to commute these sentences, but having the power to do something does not mean the people most profoundly affected by it should be treated as an afterthought," he continued. "At a minimum, these families deserved notice, respect and an opportunity to be heard before such a consequential decision was announced."
news.summary: Sunny Hostin and Ana Navarro were split over Newsom's 548 death row commutations, and Navarro argued that Gov. Gavin Newsom should have notified the families.
news.author: Hanna Panreck

news.title: Black Voters Swung the South. Their Message to Democrats: Don’t Squander This.
news.text:
After a slew of historic firsts on November 3, including the election of the first Black woman governor in US history, Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms, the internet was flooded with posts crediting Stacey Abrams, the first Black woman to run for governor on a major-party ticket, with helping make Democrats’ big wins in the South possible. 

About a week later, Abrams received her flowers for real at Facing Race, the country’s largest multiracial racial justice conference, in Raleigh, North Carolina. At the center of Facing Race was people power—and what to do with it next.

On Thursday—the day after Senator-elect Scott Colom was declared the winner of a race that will make him Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction—thousands of community organizers, public servants, artists, and activists gathered for three days in the home of the South’s oldest historically Black college, Shaw University, birthplace of the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee.

The mood in Raleigh was celebratory yet cautious, as racial justice practitioners took stock of their hard-fought victories while preparing for the battles ahead, including the need for ongoing resistance to authoritarianism and greater political investment in the South.

“I ended up being extremely proud of what we were able to see in Alabama and especially across the South,” said Tamela Glover, a 39-year-old native of Selma and organizer with the nonprofit Alabama Rise. In Glover’s home state, House Rep. Shomari Figures was resoundingly reelected in a district that the state GOP redrew to try and oust him. “But I also know that we can’t just celebrate. The real work begins with holding everybody accountable.”

Facing Race’s location and theme—“rooted in resistance, powered by solidarity”—were chosen long before Democrats flipped North Carolina’s state House and ended a GOP supermajority in the state Senate, former North Carolina Gov. Roy Cooper flipped an open Senate seat, and Democrats flipped several House seats redistricted to favor Republicans: a map drawn to secure Republicans an 11-3 split in North Carolina’s House delegation is now poised to end up 11-3 for Democrats.

“It’s great to celebrate the wins we saw,” said Glenn Harris, the president of Race Forward, the nonprofit that organizes Facing Race. “But the thing that we can always celebrate is the history of Black organizing in this country.”

“Using North Carolina as an example,” Harris said, “that was not just about what’s happening in the political moment. That was about years of building statewide infrastructure that allowed folks to take advantage of that moment.”

Friday kicked off with a keynote address by Abrams, who briefly outlined her rise to national prominence: beginning in 2018, when she narrowly lost the Georgia gubernatorial race to then–Georgia Secretary of State Brian Kemp, whom President Trump later repudiated for refusing to help him rig Georgia’s 2020 election results. The same year, Abrams founded Fair Fight Action, a nonprofit dedicated to fighting voter suppression—a practice her opponent had been accused of by multiple civil rights groups in a 2018 lawsuit. Abrams and Kemp faced off again in 2022. Abrams has since launched numerous other initiatives to fight authoritarianism and protect diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. (“I’m basically the Costco of democracy,” Abrams said during her keynote.)

A couple of days before Facing Race, Abrams published a Substack newsletter titled “After the Wave, the Work,” in which she noted that despite Democrats’ new majorities in both chambers of Congress, Republicans still controlled the executive and judicial branches. We’re “living through,” Abrams wrote, what political scientists Steve Levitsky and Lucan Way call “competitive authoritarianism,” where certain components of democracy like elections continue imperfectly while the party in power exploits and redraws the government’s institutions in their favor. 

In her keynote address on Friday, Abrams laid out a ten-step framework for understanding how authoritarianism occurs and characterized the current “moment of opportunity” as a “time where people have been so angry that they could not keep their voices contained, where they were so outraged by the outrage of the Supreme Court to strip us of our voting rights that they showed up anyway.”

Spurred by the Supreme Court’s erosion of the Voting Rights Act in April’s Louisiana v. Callais decision, which gave the go-ahead for GOP-controlled legislatures to gerrymander majority-Black districts in the South out of existence, droves of Black voters showed up to the ballot box and voted overwhelmingly for Democrats.

“They proved that participation does not eliminate discrimination,” Abrams said. “But they were never going to let it stop them from having the patience and the perseverance to make change.”

According to the Nationhood Lab, a project of Salve Regina University’s Pell Center, CNN exit polls showed democracy was a top voter concern—behind only the economy—in Georgia, South Carolina, Mississippi, and Florida, where Democrats made significant gains.

In my conversations with the people attending Facing Race—from the Deep South; to the nation’s capital, which just elected its first democratic socialist mayor; to Midwestern cities that were the sites of aggressive ICE operations and powerful resistance—all emphasized that they saw the midterm victories as merely a starting point for defending democracy. 

Andrea Pérez-Maikkula, a 43-year-old DEI practitioner born in Puerto Rico and living in Minnesota, said she was excited about the blue wave, especially Peggy Flanagan’s Minnesota Senate win, making Flanagan the first Native American woman to secure election to the upper chamber. 

But Pérez-Maikkula is also “concerned about what’s going to happen when the excitement dies down,” adding, “If we just stay complacent with the results alone, we’re not going to be in a good place a couple of years from now.”

Another consensus was that Democrats could have won even bigger prizes had they invested more in races in the South previously considered long shots. 

Cultural critic, sociologist, and University of North Carolina Center for Information, Technology and Public Life professor Tressie McMillan Cottom, another keynote speaker, challenged the prevailing assumption in the media and in national Democratic circles that rural means white. According to a Politico analysis of initial election data, majority Black counties in the South saw “the greatest surges in turnout this cycle compared to the 2022 midterms.”

Cottom also spoke about Democrats’ neglect of the South, naming Florida—where state Rep. Angie Nixon, the Democratic Senate nominee, lost by less than three percentage points to Republican incumbent Sen. Ashley Moody—as a prime example of a lost opportunity for Democrats.

“People are being very hesitant in terms of funding Black women, especially in the South,” Nixon herself told MS NOW weeks before the midterms, arguing that Florida isn’t a “red state; it is an underinvested state.”

Nixon won the state’s most populous county, Miami-Dade, by more than seven points, defying all expectations for a self-proclaimed democratic socialist in a place where the label “communist”—which has more negative resonance in Miami than perhaps anywhere else in the country—was relentlessly weaponized against her. (Then–Vice President Kamala Harris lost Miami-Dade in 2024 by more than one and a half times that margin.) Nixon has suggested that she’ll run again in 2028.

Up until the week before the election, Black and Latino lawmakers, and their allies, were arguing that they needed more funding from the national party. While the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee and Senate Majority PAC poured large sums of money into competitive races in other parts of the country, critics said their funding of Senate candidates in the South was too little, too late. 

The Senate Majority PAC and its affiliates, reportedly gave $150 million to Sherrod Brown in Ohio, $67 million to Josh Turek in Iowa, and the same amount to Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan—after Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer and the establishment initially hesitated to embrace him; $65 million to Troy Jackson in Maine; and tens of millions more for races in Texas and Kansas. 

But Colom received just $2.2 million from SMP for Mississippi, and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews just $750,000. Nixon, in Florida, and Jamie Davis in Louisiana—who both ran stunningly close Senate races in Republican strongholds—seemingly went without any direct funding at all.

Davis, like Colom, would have become his state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction; he lost by less than two points.

Just days after his win, Colom—whose national funding mainly consisted of a modest last-minute injection of ad money—told NBC’s Meet the Press: “In the South, we had to do more with less. In Mississippi, we got it out the mud,” adding that “what we need to do now as a Democratic Party is understand we can’t continue to allow that lack of investment.”

As Adam Mahoney of Capital B pointed out, some of the country’s closest Senate races were those in Louisiana, Florida, Mississippi, and South Carolina, where the Democratic establishment spent significantly less on advertising than in other races.

The ongoing work of building multiracial democracy came up again and again; Abrams emphasized it towards the end of her speech with an impassioned call for attendees to hold their newly elected officials to account.

“We’ve got to start showing up in their offices and reminding them of their intention,” Abrams said. “We’ve got to write bills for them and make sure we find voters for them. We’ve got to find the power and the confidence for them. We’ve got to find them courage while we’re at it, because they are going to start to believe that these seats are theirs and not yours.”
news.summary: After a slew of historic firsts on November 3, including the election of the first Black woman governor in US history, Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms, the internet was flooded with posts crediting Stacey Abrams, the first Black woman to run for governor on a major-party ticket, with helping make Democrats’ big wins in the South […]

news.title: Rising star among Democrats becomes the new frontrunner for 2028 nod
news.text:
There is a new favorite on the Democratic side for 2028 - months before campaigning to be the next president begins. 

Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff has emerged as the early frontrunner among potential Democratic candidates for the 2028 presidential election, following a decisive midterm re-election victory and a new national survey showing him ahead of several prominent party figures.

At 39, Ossoff is the youngest member of the U.S. Senate. Political observers view his age as a potential asset for the Democratic Party following two consecutive presidential cycles heavily focused on the age and health of Donald Trump and Joe Biden, as reported by The Daily Beast.

Ossoff recently secured another Senate term in Georgia — a state Trump won in 2024 — by defeating Republican challenger Mike Collins. Throughout that campaign, Ossoff frequently criticized Trump and his allies over rising inflation, the war in Iran and allegations of corruption, drawing frequent comparisons to former President Barack Obama for his speaking style.

Despite his current polling position, Ossoff has stated that he does not intend to run for the White House in 2028, though political commentators have noted that Obama made similar denials before launching his 2008 campaign. 

Few officials candidates for 2028 have announced their intentions, but several prominent names are being used for both sides of the political aisle. 

For Democrats, Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Governor Gavin Newsom and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg have all said they will make decisions soon, while former Vice President Kamala Harris has indicated she is considering another bid.

Data from the Emerson College national poll illustrates a shifting landscape among Democratic voters as the party prepares to take control of both chambers of Congress after the midterms. When respondents were asked without prompts whom they would like to see as the 2028 Democratic nominee, 16 percent named Ossoff. Ocasio-Cortez placed second at 12 percent, followed by Newsom at 8 percent, while Harris and Buttigieg tied at 6 percent.

When presented with a list of specific candidates, Ossoff maintained a narrower lead with 17 percent support. Harris followed closely at 16 percent, Ocasio-Cortez received 15 percent and Buttigieg garnered 14 percent. 

While support for Ossoff and Ocasio-Cortez has grown, polling numbers for other established figures have declined, with Newsom’s support dropping by 16 percentage points over the last year and Harris’s backing falling by 31 percentage points since her 2024 presidential election loss to Trump.

Following their midterm gains, congressional Democrats are preparing to launch oversight investigations into Trump and his administration regarding the Iran conflict and alleged corruption as they look ahead to the next presidential race. 

On the Republican side, the 2028 field also remains unsettled. Although Vice President JD Vance has widely been viewed as the natural successor to Trump, the same Emerson College open-ended survey found Secretary of State Marco Rubio leading Vance among respondents, 36 percent to 20 percent.
news.summary: The 2028 campaign for president will soon begin and a new frontrunner has emerged on the Democratic side
news.author: Jasmine Fernández

news.title: The Babylon Bee Trolled GTA 6, and a Left-Wing News Outlet Took the Bait
news.text:
The world is abuzz over Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6, which came out on Thursday. It has been one of the most anticipated new releases in a long time, and it’s the talk of social media.

Confession: I’m not a gamer, and I only have a passing familiarity with the GTA franchise. So I asked Grok to summarize the premise of the game.

“The official premise is simple and classic GTA: Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos have always known ‘the deck is stacked against them,’” Grok explained. “When an easy score goes wrong, the pair are dropped into a criminal conspiracy that stretches across the entire state of Leonida, forcing them to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive.”

Leonida is a stand-in for Florida, and the game’s visuals have a sunny, Miami-influenced vibe. People have noticed some nuggets that sound like there’s a conservative streak in the plotline of the game itself.

Warning: video game violence.

NEW: In GTA 6, left-wing protesters demand a bear be freed from captivity, then it immediately mauls them to death. It’s resulting in mass backlash from the Left. The developers are genius 🤣 https://t.co/uTZ9vaw04Y— Jack (@jackunheard) November 18, 2026

The Babylon Bee got in on the hype with a parody version of GTA called Grand Faith Auto. Its setting is a place called New Mercy, where you, as the player, earn divine-approval stars for doing good deeds. Eventually, Satan pursues you as well. It’s a free, browser-based game.

Related: Hulvey Canceled a Sold-Out Concert Rather Than Compromise His Faith

It should be painfully obvious to everyone that it’s a parody, right? Not so fast. The “news outlet” Headquarters, which came out of the Kamala Harris campaign, thinks it’s legit and that conservatives have come up with an alternative to GTA 6.

Republicans announce a “Christian alternative” to GTA 6 called “Grand Faith Auto.” They are reportedly boycotting the wildly popular game because they claim it encourages violence. https://t.co/VhctyB3feP— Headquarters (@HQNewsNow) November 19, 2026

How dense can these people be? It’s from The Babylon Bee, for crying out loud! Then again, the left has fallen for the Bee’s satire plenty of other times before.

Side note: For the most part, I love The Babylon Bee and have for years. But I take major umbrage at its constant low-hanging fruit portrayal of Waffle House as a place where trashy people fight all the time.

Grand Faith Auto is a parody on at least two levels. Obviously, it’s making fun of the GTA franchise and its propensity for violence and rewarding users for committing that violence within the game. But it’s also a satire on Christian entertainment that’s second-tier and of poorer quality. It makes the point that we Christians should expect more from our entertainment and not just cheesy alternative versions of the world’s diversions. (I also can’t help but think that the star-earning component of the game may also be a parody of works-based theology.)

Ultimately, nobody earns God's favor by racking up enough good-deed stars, and nobody earns journalistic credibility by mistaking a Babylon Bee joke for an actual Republican initiative. The Bee managed to lampoon a video game and cheesy Christian knockoffs. Then Headquarters showed up and unwittingly turned itself into the final boss.

news.title: The Democrats who would be 'king' of the United States
news.text:
O’Rourke raised $6.1m (€5.5m) in the first 24 hours of his presidential campaign. By November 2019, the money had slowed, an Iowa poll had him at 1%, and he was struggling to qualify for the next debate. He quit before a single primary vote had been cast. 

The man who would eventually beat Donald Trump was Joe Biden, whom plenty of Democrats already thought was too old. Biden went on to prove them wrong in 2020, but later proved them right, while giving them ample time to reconsider in 2024.

Now, the Democrats have won a Senate race in Texas and taken both houses of Congress. They gained nine Senate seats, their biggest mid-term haul since 1958. By all means, the Democrats can celebrate, but should credit the electorate. 

The voters gave Trump a kicking, and the Democrats just happened to be on the ballot when they did. How much of that support can the Democrats call their own? We’ll know when they have to ask for it again.

Which brings us to the Texan who actually won: James Talarico did what O’Rourke couldn’t. The former middle-school teacher and Texas state representative took about 55% of the vote, against Republican attorney general Ken Paxton, becoming the first Democrat to win a US Senate election in Texas since 1988.

Gina Hinojosa also won, beating three-term governor Greg Abbott. Texans were in the mood to change more than their senator.

James Talarico can sound like a Republican, the kind that used to beat Democrats in Texas. He’s training to be a Presbyterian pastor and can talk about his faith without sounding like an aide has reminded him to mention it in the third paragraph. And he talks about what he thinks Christianity asks of the rich.

He wants higher taxes on billionaires and corporations, a public health insurance option, and federal protection for abortion rights. He opposed private-school vouchers. He has an ease with voters who Democrats often struggle to reach. His politics come from the Christian left.

In 2028, he will still be in his first Senate term. So was Barack Obama when he ran for president, a fact that will be repeated until everyone involved forgets how exceptional Obama was. Give Talarico a year in Washington and we might know more about the fights he picks when there’s a vote attached.

In Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed beat Republican Mike Rogers and will become the first Muslim US senator. The son of Egyptian immigrants, he went from a heavy defeat in the 2018 Democratic primary for governor to winning statewide on a platform that included universal healthcare and sharp criticism of Israel. The American Israel public affairs committee spent nearly $30m (€27m) opposing him. And Michigan went for Trump in 2024.

El-Sayed’s victory there makes it harder to dismiss a progressive on the grounds that swing-state voters will automatically recoil. A presidential run would bring opposition on a scale far beyond the Michigan race, and quite a bit of that opposition may come from within his own party. He may have more immediate influence over what the candidates are asked about Gaza and healthcare than over whose name ends up on the ballot.

And since somebody will ask about Zohran Mamdani, the New York mayor was born in Uganda and became a US citizen through naturalisation in 2018. The US constitution requires a president to be a natural-born citizen.

A US citizen from birth can qualify, even if born abroad. Mamdani can still have a say in what Democrats talk about, especially when the conversation turns to what it costs to live in the cities they run.

Of the younger Democrats, Jon Ossoff looks the likeliest to make a serious bid. At 39, the Georgia senator has already won twice in a state Trump carried in 2024. He raised more than $100m (€91m) for his re-election campaign and went after Trump over the use of public office for private gain.

The ability to raise money and carry a state that Democrats could need in 2028 puts him ahead of people who have spent years telling the party how to win one.

And then there’s Kamala Harris. In one national poll this week, Harris led the prospective Democratic presidential field. In another, Ossoff led her by a point. Harris has a constituency and the advantage of being the name people recognise when a pollster rings two years out.

Harris had three months to make her case in 2024. She inherited Biden’s campaign and much of his baggage. When ABC’s The View asked what she’d have done differently to him, she had her chance. “There is not a thing that comes to mind,” she said. You could attribute that to loyalty to the man who made her vice-president, or arrogance married to incompetence. It was a hell of a thing to offer voters who wanted a change of government. She went on to lose all seven battleground states.

Harris — unapologetic for the administration’s role in the genocide in Gaza — will undoubtedly make the case that she’d run a different campaign given a full primary. The party, surely, owes itself and its beleaguered supporters an imagination. 

After a mid-term in which voters backed Democrats of very different stripes, going straight back to Harris would suggest the party has no ears, but a gargantuan ego.

California governor Gavin Newsom has the visibility and hubris for a fight. Andy Beshear has twice won the governorship of Kentucky as a Democrat. There are choices, albeit quite morally dubious choices.

The Republicans, too, have decisions to make. The first one is how much of Trump they want to keep. Vice-president JD Vance and secretary of state Marco Rubio are the obvious, but tainted, frontrunners. If the party wanted someone who could do for it what Talarico did for the Democrats, it could look to Vermont. Republican Phil Scott has just won a sixth term as governor in a state Harris carried by nearly 32 points. One of those Harris votes was his.

There’s little sign he wants to run for president. And the fact he can persuade Democrats to vote for him might be the first thing held against him in a Republican primary.

If you were picking a Democrat to watch in the primaries, you’d pick Ossoff. If you wanted to kid yourself the party was actually learning something, you’d spend more time listening to Talarico and El-Sayed.

As for Beto O’Rourke, he went home to the Lone Star state and lost another election, to Abbott in 2022. He kept registering voters through his group, Powered by People. In 2019, Joe Hagan returned to El Paso to ask O’Rourke if he might be president. 

Last month, he went back to ask him how Democrats had finally won Texas. In the meantime, Beto, in continuing to register voters, had done the one thing his party has so often refused to do: Listened.
news.summary: The party swept the mid-terms because voters wanted to punish Donald Trump, not because its candidates were so remarkable. There is no obvious frontrunner ahead of 2028, writes Colin Sheridan
news.author: Colin Sheridan,Irishexaminer.com

news.title: Finding the anti-Trump: The Democratic contenders for president in 2028
news.text:
It was still election night at the midterms when pundits started talking about the presidential race in 2028.

It seems like a long way away, but in the never-ending world of US politics, contenders are already preparing behind the scenes for their bids for the White House.

It is considered poor form for candidates to announce a run before the midterm elections.

But in the next few months, politicians will be throwing their hats into the ring.

With no obvious frontrunner on the Democratic side, expect a lot of candidates to put up their hands.

So who are the big contenders for the job?

Kamala Harris

The most obvious candidate in presidential elections is usually the loser from last time.

Kamala Harris has repeatedly said her run was seriously hamstrung by a sudden entry into the race without a chance to introduce herself to voters.

But critics say her campaign was marked by missteps.

Both things can be true at once.

She now has the advantage of universal name recognition, but polling shows that even as people know her, they don't necessarily like her.

And it's hard to convince voters you can win an election when you've already lost.

Pete Buttigieg

If you’d been looking at political coverage in the past year, you’d be forgiven for thinking Pete Buttigieg was the most prominent candidate.

He was doing countless television and podcast interviews and holding rallies all over the US.

But Buttigieg wasn't running for election, and hasn't held elected office since leaving the mayoralty of South Bend, Indiana, in 2020.

His first run for the presidency in 2020 stunned Democratic operatives, where he overcame questions of his very thin resume by winning the Iowa caucuses.

Since then he served as Joe Biden's Secretary of Transportation, and has spent the last two years discreetly preparing a run for the presidency.

He currently leads many of the polls.

If elected he would be among the youngest presidents in history, as well as the first openly gay president.

Minutes after winning re-election to his Senate seat earlier this month, pundits were already talking about Jon Ossoff running for president.

His victory speech struck all the right notes, lambasting the Trump administration while reaching out to independent and Republican voters.

The Georgia senator with Australian roots is just 39 years old, which would make him the youngest president in US history if he was elected.

But his speeches are perfect for TikTok, frequently being spliced up in digestible clips for audiences to take in.

He has also managed thus far to appeal to both the moderate and progressive wings of the party.

But Ossoff has pledged to serve a full-term in the Senate instead of running for president.

It's the sort of promise that politicians routinely make before election day and frequently break soon afterwards.

Gavin Newsom

If Hollywood was casting someone to play the president, they would choose Gavin Newsom.

The governor of California has been doing everything he can to stay in contention for the presidency, including a visit to Ukraine this week.

And his social media antics seem purposefully designed to get under the skin of Donald Trump.

The problem seems to be that nobody wants Gavin Newsom to be president more than the man himself.

But ambition aside, the abilities that got him into arguably the second-most powerful job in America could very well get him into the most powerful.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez

For years, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has been the most talked about progressive in the United States.

And come 2028, she will finally be old enough to run for president.

The 36-year-old would enter the race with the backing of an ardent progressive voter base.

But she will have a tougher task convincing more moderate Democrats that she is mainstream enough to win a presidential election.

Ocasio-Cortez would be a groundbreaking president for several reasons - female and Hispanic, the first to identify as a democratic socialist and the youngest ever. 

Governor Josh Shapiro made a strong claim for electability when he won the crucial state of Pennsylvania by a 60-38 point margin.

And navy pilot and astronaut Mark Kelly, now the senator from Arizona, has proven he can also win a swing state.

Governors JB Pritzker, Wes Moore, Andy Beshear and Gretchen Whitmer would all have decent cases to make.

And Senators Cory Booker and Raphael Warnock are reportedly considering bids.

We will be discussing the Republican contenders for the presidential nomination next week.

news.title: Nebraska Republican Rep. Don Bacon Weighs Run for President: 'I Haven't Committed to It'
news.text:
Rep. Don Bacon (R-NE) is apparently weighing a run for president in 2028 but said Thursday he has not committed to it yet.

Bacon’s comments came during an event at the National Press Club where he said he was also thinking about supporting another candidate with the same priorities, WOWT reported.

Bacon said, “I haven’t committed to it,” when speaking of a presidential campaign, emphasizing his message of confronting the national debt, protecting Social Security and Medicare, and emphasizing governing over partisanship.

“We need an American president. We also have to realize the strength of our country is not our president — it’s not what makes us a great country. It’s not about fancy ballrooms or any of this stuff. What makes us special is that we, as Americans, have freedom. We have economic freedom. We have the Bill of Rights — and that’s why we compete and win all over the world,” he stated.

He criticized President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans for the midterm election results.

“I think it was Trump loss with an assist by the Republican Congress,” he stated.

Bacon’s comments came after Democrats swept the U.S. House and Senate during the midterms, while in Nebraska, Gov. Jim Pillen (R) secured reelection after campaigning against Democrat candidate Lynne Walz, a former state senator.

Pillen’s win came after President Donald Trump saw massive support during an October rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, according to Breitbart News.

A poll in June showed Vice President JD Vance (R) and former Vice President Kamala Harris (D) were dominating within their own parties as potential 2028 presidential candidates.

A few months later, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he had “no plans” to run for president in 2028 while also declining to rule out a future bid, and Sen. John Kennedy (R-LA) said in October he was thinking about running for president, Breitbart News reported.

news.text:
Lawrence appeared on the show with her Hunger Games co-star Josh Hutcherson when Cohen had the Oscar winner play “Plead the Fifth,” in which she was asked a series of tough questions and could skip only one. The Bravo host asked Lawrence to rank Hutcherson, Liam Hemsworth, Chris Pratt, Timothée Chalamet, and Bradley Cooper. 

Before she answered, Lawrence nervously demurred, “OK, I guess I’ll go—I mean, they were all so amazing.” Hutcherson laughed in response. 

She then named Hutcherson first and MAGA-friendly star Pratt last. 

“Best is Josh, and then, OK, Hemsworth, Cooper, Chalamet, Pratt,” she answered.

Lawrence, 36, starred with Pratt, 47, in the 2016 space-themed romantic drama Passengers. The film was a major box-office success, made on an estimated budget of $100-150 million and garnering $303 million during its theatrical run.

Lawrence has expressed discomfort about having to act out sex scenes with Pratt in the film, saying that it was a “bizarre experience” and noting that her co-star was married (at the time, Pratt was with actress Anna Faris). 

“I had my first real sex scene a couple weeks ago, and it was really bizarre, it was really weird,” Lawrence confessed during a Hollywood Reporter actor’s roundtable in 2015. “Everything was done right, it wasn’t anybody’s fault, nobody did anything wrong, it’s just a bizarre experience.”

“It was going to be my first time even kissing a married man, and guilt is like the worst feeling in your stomach,” the actress explained, referring to Pratt. “I knew it was my job, but I couldn’t tell my stomach.”

Pratt, who is now married to Katherine Schwarzenegger, has long made headlines for his dubious political leanings. He has defended his cousin-in-law and U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s dangerous health movement; touted the importance of not taking sides in the divisive 2024 election between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris; and been called out by actor Elliot Page for his “infamously anti lgbtq” church.”

Despite Lawrence’s assessment of her on-screen kiss with Pratt, critics lauded their chemistry in Passengers.

The No Hard Feelings star has previously been candid about the awkwardness of kissing her co-stars, especially those who she is close to in real life. In January, the actress was asked about the act in Die My Love, in which she starred opposite Robert Pattinson. She said it was “easier” to kiss Pattinson on-screen because the pair “did not know each other” well at the time.

“Like in Hunger Games, like me and Josh Hutcherson would have to kiss and that’s like… Imagine it,” she said in a conversation with 92NY. “You know, it’s weirder and so yeah, doing it with a stranger is preferable.”

She concluded that acting can be “very embarrassing.”

news.title: The Mechanical Reason Why Republicans Lost the Midterms
news.text:
Everybody has written a think piece about "why Republicans lost" so badly in the elections, including me. 

It's what we do, partly because it is our job, but mostly because we like it. Writers like to think about the "big picture," dive into motivations and connections, explore big ideas, and find patterns hidden in the chaos. 

Then there are the data guys, whose job and passion is to measure things. People like me often depend on them, but because they focus on the mundane mechanics, we also tend to use them as research assistants in our own minds. 

We're the theoreticians; they're the experimental guys, digging into what the world actually tells us. And Quantus Insights is sharing some interesting data we really ought to consider and work into our "BigThink" pieces, because actual data has to ground our theories, or they are just intellectual onanism. We can love our pet theories all we want, but without data...it's just sophomores talking in the lounge. 

Of every 100 Trump 2024 voters, about 63 voted Republican, 4 voted Democratic, and 33 stayed home. Of every 100 Harris voters, about 85 voted Democratic. Very few people switched and about a third of one side sat out. https://t.co/qrHxTerxhg— Quantus Insights (@QuantusInsights) November 19, 2026

So what does the Quantus research show? On the one hand, it tells us something we already sorta knew: Democrats showed up, and Republicans didn't this election. 

The turnout differences between Kamala Harris voters and Donald Trump voters are very stark. Only 63 percent of Trump voters bothered to show up at the polls and vote Republican this time, and while only a few Trump voters switched parties, they were in key demographics the Republicans have to get back or it will spell trouble. 

The voters who did switch were the newest part of the 2024 coalition: young men and Latino voters. Men under 30 moved 32 points toward Democrats. Latino men moved 27. https://t.co/eoZA6UTGfj— Quantus Insights (@QuantusInsights) November 19, 2026

And it wasn't just squishes who sat this one out: it was key parts of the Trump coalition, who may or may not be disaffected, as the younger men likely were when they switched; they were just uninterested or even annoyed enough to sit this one out. They didn't vote Democrat; they voted "a pox on both your houses."

For some — relatively few, I would guess — it was direct annoyance or anger at the fact that Trump went to war with Iran, but for the majority it was about the downstream effects of the war: the economic pain from rising prices. For them, it looked like Trump took his eye off the ball or followed policies that hurt them. 

The polls had the direction right but missed the size of the outcome. Democrats beat their final averages by about 4 points nationally, and by 8 to 9 in Texas, Georgia and the Carolinas. The miss was largest where the turnout gap was largest. https://t.co/rKCwlJ6FOr— Quantus Insights (@QuantusInsights) November 19, 2026

As always, in elections, turnout matters more than almost anything else. The choices of Independent voters often swing big national elections, but the base votes for each party, and how enthusiastic the partisan voters are to show up, matter the most in off-year elections. 

Here, not many Republican voters or independents who voted Republican shifted, but a lot of Republicans didn't show up, and that made all the difference in the world. If you want to know why the Democrats took reliably Red states this year, it all comes down to the fact that Democrats showed up at presidential-election levels out of hatred for Trump, and the Trump voters, in large numbers, did not. Many Republicans sat it out. 

The country swung hard from 2024. But it wasn't about a collective change of mind more so as it was one side showed up nearly at full force, and the other did not. A majority of voters, 52%, viewed the Democratic Party unfavorably on the same day they handed it Congress.— Quantus Insights (@QuantusInsights) November 19, 2026

The election was not, as Democrats would have you believe, a full-throated endorsement of Democrats so much as a rejection of, or at least a sense of disquiet about, Trump's second term. 

On the one hand, that means that almost every Democrat will be inclined to misread the election results. Most of them believe voters gave them a stamp of approval, when in fact they chose what they believed was the best of two bad choices, or made no real choice at all by sitting it out. 

Of course, to be fair, the Democrats could say the same about the 2016 and 2024 elections, where Trump won at least partly because people were not at all happy with Hillary! or Kamala! It's hard to remember any election, if any, where the country swung behind a candidate out of pure love, right?

The good news is that there was no massive shift against Republicans, even though it looked that way to a lot of people. 

The bad news is that the coalition is grumbling and the loyalty factor has waned. 

The concerning news is that the attractiveness of Republicans to potential new coalition members — Hispanics and young men — was diminished enough that they chose the Democrats this time. We need two things to get them back: the Democrats need to offend them, as they likely will, and we need a new reason for them to come back to us. 

Those of us in the talking biz can talk all we want, but we need the numbers people and the "doing" people to work on the mechanics to repair the damage. 

The damage is reparable, though. In 1982, the voters gave Ronald Reagan a spanking because the recession was raging and inflation was still high. No doubt the pundits were sure that Republicans would never recover, just as they assumed that the 1974 elections were the death knell for Republicans. 

Neither turned out to be true.

news.title: Hasan Piker Joins VF’s Fair Game: “I Am Not a Terrorist”
news.text:
This year Hasan was involved in dozens of races across the country, campaigning for progressive candidates like Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. But you’re probably more likely to associate Hasan’s name with what other people have had to say about him—from Fox News commentators to more established members of the Democratic Party.
Hasan regularly courts controversy on both his hours-long Twitch streams, where he’s said things like “America deserved 9/11,” and social media, where he’s written that Hamas “is a thousand times better than” Israel. He claims he’s often taken out of context, and that his audience knows what he really means—and where he stands. In his mind, he’s a leftist provocateur, maybe, but one who understands the importance of working-class values and electoral strategy.
While Hasan has walked back some of his more inflammatory language, his rhetoric raises the question: Is he a liability to the cause he champions? Or is he successfully reaching the critical audience—namely, young men—that helped elect the wave of progressives poised to take office in January?
With 2028 on the horizon, I wanted to know how Hasan thinks about his growing platform, and if he sees his role shifting in the media landscape. What responsibility does he have to his viewers and to the candidates he supports? And does he regret any of those past statements?
We also got into the DSA’s more extreme positions and how to make sense of them; why he thinks the Republicans put his thirst trap on the jumbotron at their convention; and how he, a self-proclaimed socialist, thinks about his own money.
Mark Guiducci: Hasan Piker, welcome to Fair Game.
Hasan Piker: Very excited to be here.
Thanks for coming. Hasan, you are more online than just about anyone. You spend at least seven hours a day streaming. You reach tens of thousands of people at a time on average, and it’s all in the channel that you control. I’m curious, what are you doing here with me today? Why are you showing up for a show with a legacy media publication? What’s in it for you?
Well, I saw the clips and everybody looked really good. The lighting was perfect. I saw the Dari[aliza Avila Chevalier] clips, I saw Ta-Nehisi [Coates], and I was like, I got to get in on that.
Okay, that’s the team then.
Yeah. So shouts out to the team. You guys did a phenomenal job lighting this up. It looks very cool too.
Okay. We’ll take the compliment.
But the serious answer is, I mean, I reach an audience that obviously does not watch television, does not read legacy publications at all. And I want to show people that read Vanity Fair that I am not a terrorist.
Right. Which brings me to my next question because—
Do you condemn Hasan Piker?
Yeah, exactly. That would be the name of the episode. You’ve been everywhere this year, and you became this kind of bogeyman for the right, who probably have never heard you, watched your stream, or heard anything you’ve said out of your mouth. They’ve just heard quotes repeated by news anchors. And not even just for the right, even for some on the left. And you played this interesting role because you were a surrogate and a media figure and then a media figure covering the media as well. I want to spend a little bit of time talking about how you see your role. And to start, do you consider yourself a journalist?

Okay. Because it’s like you present this interesting new type of figure. I was thinking about how you’ve done an interview with CNN, you’ve done interviews with MS NOW, but they don’t have you on as much as I would expect them to.
They never do.
I have some thoughts, but I wonder why you think that is.
I think I’ve pissed off a bunch of executives over there, because, in my experience, there are plenty of amazing reporters and journalists and producers that I know that work at all of these newsrooms, right? But from what I have seen, the masthead has a very different editorial slant than sometimes what the reporters want to cover.
Because they talk about you a lot.
They talk about me a lot. And also I’ve never been invited on any of these outlets as a pundit either, which is also strange because, as you also pointed to, I don’t just operate as a campaignster. As a matter of fact, that’s something I did very briefly and I did not like it at all. I’m first and foremost a commentator…. I do have the capacity to do journalism at times. I’ll do interviews with candidates. I’ll go out and—
Candidates you like.
Well, candidates I like. Sometimes I do interviews with candidates I don’t like or I’m unsure about as well. The problem is most of the candidates don’t want to come on if they know I’m gonna cook ’em. Like Gavin Newsom, I have had feelers out to get him on the broadcast.
Invite him.
I have. Gavin, Gavin, come on the show. I am a taxpaying California resident. I’m one of your constituents. You want to be president in 2028, you’re gonna have to be able to talk to people like myself.
All right. So, Hasan, this cycle you were involved in some way in, by one count, 48 different candidates’ races, and AIPAC and pro-Israel groups spent about $101 million in those races. And on Election Day, your stream was the second most watched in the country after NBC News’s “Kornacki Cam.” With a little bit of distance, how are you thinking about what happened a couple of weeks ago, both for yourself and for the country?
I feel a lot of hope. Hopefully it’s not going to be short-lived. But I feel very excited for the first time in a very long time, after 10 years of some of the most odious politics that we’ve seen from Trumpism, from MAGA. We finally saw a real sea change through electoralism. People truly have had enough with Trumpism.
Do you think MAGA’s dead?
I wouldn’t be so certain because I feel like if there’s one controlled opposition party that is capable of breathing life back into MAGA, it would be the establishment Democrats. So I’m a little bit worried, but it’s very clear that people are truly fed up.
All right. So there are a couple of different narratives that are coming out of the midterms right now. Rahm Emanuel, for instance, is touting this as a victory for moderate Democrats, saying that they ran 21 points above Kamala Harris. The DSA, meanwhile, is claiming that American voters have “emphatically endorsed socialism.” Other pundits are saying that these big gains have nothing to do with the Democrats and are actually about the war in Iran and high gas prices. So does this debate between moderates and progressives feel like a healthy back-and-forth to you, or does this feel like the new aisle that has to be straddled?
I mean, I think this is not even a new debate. This factional battle has existed within the Democratic Party and perhaps—
Yeah, but the progressive wing was always really fringe.

And now we’re talking about—I don’t know if 50/50 is right. I don’t want to use numbers, but—
I think it’s a testament to our success, especially in the midterms, that there are a lot of people who are trying to protect their comfortable sinecures and are outright panicking. And all of that completely sidesteps the reality that the vulgar Bernie-ism of 2016 was echoed through every single candidacy, every single campaign all across the country, from the obvious Berniecrats like Abdul El-Sayed to even people like Roy Cooper, who in the past were very moderate, very centrist. And he still is a center-right figure, which clearly works in North Carolina. But even he was railing against data centers, billionaires, the uncertainty surrounding AI. I mean, this is left populism. And that rhetoric, one could say, was deployed in the past by even the likes of Bill Clinton and Al Gore.

But for some strange reason, there was a turning point in 2016 where the Democratic Party adopted this strange role of defending the corporate class and defending the elites and took ownership over, I guess, defending these institutions overall. And these institutions are worthy of defending, for the record. However, from the perspective of the masses, if the government is failing them, if these institutions are failing them, then they wanted someone to break it. And that was obviously the right populism of Donald Trump. And break those institutions, he surely did. And we’ve seen the devastating results of that.
So you credit the progressivism with what happened on election night?
Absolutely. I mean, there’s certainly local moderation on issues, right? Because James Talarico went from saying “God is nonbinary” to “we need to defend our transgender brothers and sisters, our neighbors,” which is, again, insanely woke for Texas, or just in general, right? There are far more conservative figures in the party than James Talarico’s current position on the trans issue.
Okay. But sometimes the way that you run—oftentimes the way that you run needs to be different than the way that you govern or lead once you’re there. Do you think it is productive to continue pushing some of the farther-left ideas once they get to Congress? Or is pragmatism and getting things done, you know, defining things that are really achievable and sticking to them as a bloc, as a group, and pushing them over the line— when you’re talking to some of these winners, are you talking about [that]?
I think if I could speak to the entire incoming freshman class or the entire caucus—

I would say, be bold, be brave, and obviously immediately implement accountability. Investigations are an absolute must. This is what people are demanding. After the economy, the second concern, the biggest concern, is corruption. The second term with Trump has been unbelievable. I mean, look, I’m Turkish. I’ve seen corruption in the Turkish government. I’ve seen corruption and tracked it and talked about it all around the world with different governments. I’ve never seen anything like what the Trump administration has done because of how flagrant and in your face it was. And I think people responded to that, finally, in the appropriate way they should, with anger.
So you’re calling for subpoenas and investigations.
Absolutely.
Impeachment?
I think impeachment, especially for Trump, is probably the last thing that I care about. I mean, I want these guys to go to jail. Let’s be clear. If they’ve done the crime, they need to do the time. I don’t think anyone is above the law. We have to restore law and order. So I’m a law-and-order Democrat. And I know that sounds something very different in Washington, DC, or in general. I think when politicians say that, they mean, like, punish the poor for minor crimes. I’m talking about punishing the wealthy for their corruption, for their major crimes, because they’re the ones who are robbing people blind.
But, you know, a lot of people would say that impeachment would be a distraction. So I guess what I’m saying is, if you had to choose three agenda items that the Democrats are agreeing on and they’re going forward with—you already said subpoenas and investigations.

What else? What are the other two that in the first year you really want to see happen?
I think it’s virtually impossible [with] the current DOJ to—they’re not impartial, right? I don’t think that we are going to move the needle on actual criminal investigations before the Democrats win the White House in 2028. But all of this is building up for that moment. And for that reason, I think we need to talk about affordability—and not just simply talk about affordability, but also explain how we’re going to solve the affordability crisis through a comprehensive legislative agenda. And one of the major issues around affordability that is oftentimes discussed as a separate thing, but it’s not, is health care. And the Democratic Party’s approach to health care has been lackluster. Even though Americans obviously overwhelmingly trust the Democrats with fixing health care or solving the problem with health care, the reality of the matter is, while the ACA was a fantastic improvement to what existed previously, it’s not enough, and we have to move the needle in a healthier direction. We have to push for a single-payer health care solution.
Would you call it Trumpcare?
I’m perfectly fine with that. I’ve joked about that for years ’cause he’s so invested. He’s such a petty despot and so narcissistic that—
Give him the name?
Yes. I have pitched this over and over again on my show. Look, you win so big with Donald Trump if you go to Donald Trump and you say, “Look, Obamacare, not the best, right? Now you get to destroy Obamacare and you get to build something else in your name. We call it Trumpcare. It’s single-payer. It’s Medicare for All.” I think he would do it.
Look at this. Bipartisan collaboration.
Yes, I’m pragmatic. I’m bipartisan.
All right, so let’s take a step back. You were talking a second ago about how Talarico was woke. And on November 4, Twitter, formerly known as X, was amazing. Memes, jokes, you know.

I said, of course, no, because I feel like it’s deeply unethical to be sponsored by a gambling company, a prediction market, while, you know, you’re engaging in news commentary. But I know that if I did not have that economic freedom, that financial freedom, I would’ve probably had to think about whether or not I’d make this ethical compromise.
So Calvin Klein would be an exception.
Yeah, that’s fine.
I’m kidding.
Calvin Klein’s fine. I mean, I take sponsorships every now and then, like gaming companies and stuff like that. If Rockstar came to me and were like, “Grand Theft Auto VI is coming out. We want to sponsor a stream,” I would fucking love that.
Some people have a number that’s like their retirement number, at which point that’s all the money they need. They close up shop and call it a day. I wonder if you have a number after which you think it would be unethical to accumulate any more. What is the maximum amount of net worth or income that you could generate after which you would feel it’s morally reprehensible?
Great question. I have no idea. I’ve never thought about it like that because there’s no world in which I will reach that number. But all the revenue that I generate goes immediately back into this broader project. It allows me to be able to travel around the country. It allows me to be able to hire people on a moment’s notice if necessary. So that’s the way I see it. I don’t have an unethical number, but I think to each their own, because I don’t want people to hear me say this and then be like, “Well, you know, you’ve collaborated with Saikat Chakrabarti. He’s a centimillionaire. You’ve talked to Tom Steyer. He’s a billionaire.” I care more about what people’s actual advocacy is and if they’re real about it or not. And I think how much they pay into certain things can show that, for sure. But anything past the point of having—not your net worth, right, but anything past the point of just having $10 million, I feel like is insane. It’s like, What are you doing? Does that make sense?
You mean cash?
Just cash in general.
Because you said you differentiate with net worth.
I differentiate it with net worth because everyone will say, “Oh, well, I have assets. I have stocks,” or whatever. But in general, if you have—

The capacity to deploy—I feel like even $10 million is too much. If you have the capacity to deploy a million dollars into something, you’re done, you’re set. I think everything past that point is outright ridiculous.
Okay. We got a number.

All right. I want to look ahead to the future because 2028 is not far away, and I think all signs would show that you’re going to be a character in that cycle. So here’s the inevitable 2028 question: Do you think the public has met the 2028 candidate that you’ll champion yet, or do you think that person is still waiting in the wings somewhere?
I mean, the top answer, obviously, since we’re doing this will-they-won’t-they thing, is AOC. Right? She is the one figure, I think, on the left that has the capacity to unite the base, and she’s competent, she’s charismatic, incredible progressive track record as a legislator, and—
Who is moving more to the center.
Well, I think all that stuff is—it’s pragmatism. I don’t think that means that she is going to come out and be like, “I am no longer in favor of the same comprehensive policy agenda that I’ve sought to advance my whole life.”
But it might mean that she wants to unite the base.
Yeah. But I don’t think you necessarily have to do compromise on the legislative front to unite the base. If I was being fully transparent, fully honest, or maybe a little harsh, my criticisms around AOC would probably be that she’s not aggressive enough and that at times she’s come across as perhaps a little too liberal, too woke, on social issues in a way that is not appealing to broad subsets of the base.
Okay. Say AOC runs but loses the primary, and you’re dealing with Josh Shapiro or Gavin Newsom or insert centrist Democrat here.
Devastating.
What do you plan to do? Do you urge your audience to get behind them?
I don’t know. I don’t know what I would do at that point. I haven’t even thought about it because I don’t think I need to think about it.

I don’t think it’s even going to be a problem.
So, I guess AOC or not, how do you want to be involved in the 2028 election?
I’m gonna do what I did in the primaries and the midterm broadly, and hopefully we’ll have a slate of hundreds of democratic socialists that will be running in every district that will be bold, that will excite the base, and that will chart a different path forward for the Democratic Party by force.
Do you think that—we’ve talked a little bit about this toxicity of the brand of Hasan Piker, which has been burnished by the right and by some on the left.

Do you think about trying to clean that up, as it were, so that you could be more helpful to whoever that progressive candidate is? Or is it more useful for you to be ethically pure, I guess, in your estimation and stay as the stick in the mud on the far left?
Look, I got to the point I got to by being honest and sometimes being hardheaded, being stubborn, but always saying the truth. And that policy’s not going to change. So I say, if this is considered too toxic for politicians to take advantage of this platform, then they’ll lose. Because my goal is not to change myself. My goal is to change politics. I want American politics to be more responsive, not only to our demands, but also reflective of our anger as well. I truly believe that we are in the moral majority. People who look at the current system and say, “This is not helping,” people who look at their insurance premiums going up and say, “We need to change this,” that is a morally righteous fury that people feel, and there is a great deal of time and effort spent on mainstream outlets, legacy publishers in the media broadly, to try to quiet that frustration. I believe that I have a more honest approach to the matter, and that is precisely the reason why my audience continues to grow as their audience continues to age out or diminish.
I want to end on a slightly different note. I want to do a lightning round with you. I’m gonna say a series of names and I just want you to give me word association, the first thing that comes to your mind—just don’t say their job. It’s too boring.

Okay. Jensen Huang.

Jon Ossoff.
Oh, now I—fat-ass.
Megan Romer.

Hakeem Jeffries.
Oh, there’s so many directions I can go with this. Do I joke? Do I fib? Do I say what I honestly think?
You just gave me a whole speech about being honest.
Well, on my broadcast, I joke and I call him the “sex panther” because he’s so uncharismatic, but I joke and say, “Oh my God, he’s so hot. He’s so charismatic every time he comes out and delivers this speech, finger-wagging speech.” But the serious answer, the one-word serious answer, would be corrupt.
Stephen Miller.

Elizabeth Holmes.

Kim Kardashian.
Shit. Damn it. That works for Kim too.
I thought you were gonna say the same thing.
I don’t want to repeat. I don’t want to repeat. Kim Kardashian, white feminist.
Nick Fuentes.
Oh damn. I used “manlet” for Stephen Miller. Can I use multiple words for Nick Fuentes?

Gay Mexican manlet neo-Nazi.
MacKenzie Scott.

Formerly Bezos.
Yeah, yeah. Please give me money. Fund the DSA.

Ooh, a lot of deployment of the word “manlet” today. No, he’s ape.
All right. Okay, to end, I want to do a round of the Proust Questionnaire. So this is the longtime back page of the magazine. They’re small but poignant questions that say a lot about you. So are you ready?

Okay. Hasan, what is your greatest extravagance?
Ooh, that’s a good one. I can’t say my house because I feel like it’s very expensive, but it’s expensive because of the housing market in Los Angeles. So I’ll say business class travel.
Okay. What’s your most marked characteristic?
I don’t know. Probably my looks.
On what occasion do you lie?
That’s a good question. Let me think. I have to dig deep for this one. When do I lie? When I have to be polite.
What is your greatest regret?
I don’t have any regrets. I mean, you asked me about the things that I’ve said, if I regret them. I feel like I have a policy of just bouldering through the pressure and just pushing through, no matter what happens, because there’s no use crying over spilled milk. So when things happen and they’re devastating, I think about it. I feel like there are different ways that I could have gone about things and how I manage them, but ultimately I’m stronger on the other side.
You learn from it.
I learn from it. I’m stronger on the other side because of it. So I don’t really regret anything.
When and where were you happiest?
Zohran victory party 2025 was peak. Even the Bluenami was really good, but I think that was so significant for me because it was the first time I had approached a campaign hands-on and played somewhat of a role in that victory. And I was surrounded by all these people that were door knockers that had worked on the campaign. They were coming up and they’re like, “Dude, I’m here, we’re all here, because I saw Zohran on your stream, and I was like, This guy is the truth, this guy’s the real deal. And then we knocked on millions of doors.” And I felt so proud. I felt like there was a real impact that my community had made in this race in some small sense of the word.
Hasan Piker, thank you very much for coming on Fair Game.
Thank you for having me.
