news.title: 2028 Is Looking Like 2016 but Upside Down
news.text:
The two parties' presidential lineups look a lot like those of the 2015-16 cycle — in reverse.

Republicans emerged from the 2014 midterm elections with large congressional majorities (247 House members and 54 senators). Democrats have emerged from this year's midterm elections with even larger ones (259 House members and 56 senators).

But Democrats then, like Republicans now, had a much smaller field of prospective presidential candidates. Two figures in former President Barack Obama's party towered over the others in visibility and popularity — his vice president, Joe Biden, and his first-term secretary of state, Hillary Clinton.

Recent vice presidents had won the presidency or come close, among them Richard Nixon, Hubert Humphrey, George H.W. Bush and Al Gore. No former secretary of state had won the presidency since James Buchanan in 1856. Yet Obama favored Clinton over Biden.

One reason may have been age. Clinton would have been 69 at the outset of the next presidential term, while Biden would have been 74. That didn't prevent Biden from becoming the consensus choice for the nomination four years later. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), who was 75 by the next inauguration, was even older. He entered the primaries from stage left, winning 22 primaries and caucuses and holding Clinton to a 55 percent-43 percent advantage in votes cast for the nomination.

Today's Republican field looks as small as the Democratic field did at the same point in that cycle. It, too, includes a vice president and a secretary of state, with room for a third candidate who is no one's idea of a Washington insider.

Vice President JD Vance is in his first term, while Biden was in his second, and Vance's two years in the Senate pale beside Biden's 36. But Vance has the advantage of youth. He will be just 44 on Inauguration Day in 2029. Like Clinton, Secretary of State Marco Rubio served in the Senate — 14 years in his case, eight in hers. If elected in 2028, he would take the presidential oath at the mature but hardly elderly age of 57.

Rubio's statement that he won't run if Vance does can be read as an attempt to avoid turmoil in the Trump administration — a predictably unattainable goal. In the two weeks since the election, Vance has attributed the Republican rout solely to military action against Iran, which Rubio has supported. President Donald Trump, in turn, has publicly ordered Vance to give his full attention to exposing Democratic corruption in large cities.

Trump's favor may shift, and it may count for less than it once did. The Republican polling firm Echelon Insights reports that 56 percent of Republicans see themselves as party-first and only 36 percent as Trump-first. Another 51 percent say it is time to "move beyond the Trump approach."

The RealClearPolitics average of seven polls on the Republican nomination this fall shows Vance leading Rubio by a less-than-overwhelming margin, 37 percent to 28 percent. Outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis (R-FL) draws 10 percent.

DeSantis' record of policy success in Florida, the only one of the 10 largest states to remain safely Republican this year, could make him a serious contender. He would be just 50 on Inauguration Day in 2029.

Meanwhile, Democrats, still giddy over their success, could field as many presidential candidates as the 10 Republicans who competed in the 2016 caucuses and primaries. That Republican field included senators from Florida, Kentucky and Texas; current and former governors from Arkansas, Florida, New Jersey and Ohio; a pediatric surgeon from Maryland; a former tech CEO from California; and a real estate developer and reality TV host from New York.

Trump won that crowded contest despite taking positions on trade, war and economic policy far outside those of previous Republican presidents. By the time he won an outright majority in any state, 36 states had already voted.

The Democratic field now taking shape looks something like that Republican field. The RealClearPolitics average of recent polls shows measurable support for 10 candidates. They include governors from California, Illinois, Kentucky and Pennsylvania, senators from Arizona, Georgia and New Jersey, a House member from New York, a former transportation secretary, and former Vice President Kamala Harris, the party's 2024 nominee.

They range widely in age and experience. If Harris took the presidential oath in January 2029, she would be the eighth-oldest person to do so for the first time. Just days would separate her from Zachary Taylor and George H.W. Bush. Only William Henry Harrison, Buchanan, Ronald Reagan, Trump and Biden were older than all three when they first took office. At the other end of the list, either Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), at 41, or Democrat Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14), at 39, would be the youngest president ever.

The field could grow or shrink. Someone whose candidacy seems as improbable as Trump's did a dozen years ago could enter the race and win.

America's two political parties have retained their basic characters across centuries. The Republican Party has always centered on people who see themselves, and whom others see, as typical Americans. In a nation that has always been culturally diverse, they have never made up a majority on their own.

The Democrat Party has always been a coalition of outsiders, people who see themselves, and whom others see, as outside the American mainstream. If they hold together, they can form a majority.

When Democrats lack a dominant leader — and Obama, nearly 10 years out of office, no longer seems to play that role — the danger is that the party's disparate constituencies will extract concessions that help candidates win the nomination but cost them votes in the general election.

Transgender advocates' demand for sex-change surgery for prisoners, which Harris docilely endorsed on camera, wounded her candidacy in 2024, perhaps fatally. Other demands from the period Ocasio-Cortez called "Woke 1" included defunding the police, admitting all otherwise illegal aliens who claim asylum, allowing biological men in girls' sports and women's prisons, and requiring masks during the COVID-19 pandemic. Endorsing such demands may help candidates win support in the spring 2028 primaries but prove disastrous in the general election.

Democrats will have a hard time balancing public demands for "affordability" with calls for more public spending from teachers unions and victims' groups. Continued demands for racial quotas and preferences in hiring and political districting may also seem beside the point. The country elected a black president in 2008, and voters just elected a Black Democrat senator in Mississippi and a Black Republican governor in Florida.

In days of yore, local Democratic bosses could grant concessions on some issues and mollify those whose demands they rejected. Today, the very existence of single-issue groups — and their payrolls — depends on wresting concessions from the party on unpopular issues. Popular positions usually don't need paid advocates.

As analysts have noted, most voters in the electorate that gave Democrats large majorities still view the party unfavorably. In the midterm elections, voters could use Democrats as a check on an increasingly disconnected Trump without giving the party full control of the government. In 2028, Democrats will ask for just that, while voters will likely see little risk of Republicans winning the presidency and both chambers of Congress, as they did in 2016 and 2024.

That's why Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston, who have been giving Democrats good advice for more than 30 years, write that "the midterms say little about who will win in 2028" and "do not conclusively show which kind of Democrat would be more electable at the national level in 2028."

Democrats are fortunate that their majorities are large enough to limit the leverage of the Democratic Socialists of America and other leftists in setting policy. But the left has a cheering section in the press and among affluent college graduates, who lately have been the party's largest constituency. Both groups will likely push the party leftward.

None of this is set in stone. Choices yet to be made and events yet to occur will shape the outcome, as they did 10 years ago. Democrats have an opportunity to present an attractive face, but they have flubbed such opportunities before. Republicans, for all their drubbing this year, still have assets that Trump, busy redesigning the White House complex and cleaning the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, has left undeployed.

Michael Barone is a senior political analyst for the Washington Examiner, resident fellow at the American Enterprise Institute and longtime co-author of The Almanac of American Politics. news.title: Goodbye Electoral College, Hello Totalitarianism, Part One
news.text:
As we all know, the Democratic Party wants to abolish the Electoral College (EC). They might make a big push in the next two years to do so, and it is not impossible that they will succeed. Most Americans are totally clueless about why our Founders established the Electoral College, a matter I will fully discuss in part two of this series. The Democrats are trying to make it all about “democracy” now — which, in one sense, it is, and they might be able to demagogue enough people into abolishing the EC.

Technically, since the Electoral College is part of the election process and ensconced in the Constitution, the Democrats would need a constitutional amendment to abolish it. Technically. In this regard, the problem for them is that they would need 38 states to ratify the amendment, and they almost assuredly don’t have that many at present, and it will probably be several years, at best, before they could muster that number. Most Southern and Western states (minus the Left Coast) would not go for the abolition of the EC by constitutional amendment. So, the Democrats have decided to try an end run around the EC.

They have created this monstrosity called the “National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.” This thing has been around for well over a decade now, and it might be gaining steam. The idea is to find a way to elect the president by popular vote and bypass the EC (if it can’t be eradicated by constitutional amendment). What the NPVIC says is that any state would give all its electoral votes to the candidate who received the most national popular votes, even if that candidate did not win that state’s popular vote. For example, if candidate “A” won the national popular vote, he would get all of a state’s electoral votes even if candidate “B” actually won the state’s popular vote. The state’s “electors” would then be required to vote for candidate “A” when the Electoral College voted on the president. If enough states adopt the NPVIC, the Electoral College, as constitutionally construed, would be negated and bypassed.

So far, 18 states, all (unsurprisingly) very blue, and representing 222 electoral votes, have joined this compact. The newly elected Democrat governor of Nevada, Aaron Ford, hopes to get his state to enact the NPVIC. news.title: Byron Donalds Says 2028 Hopefuls Must Define Themselves, Rules Out Own Bid
news.text: Byron Donalds, Republican congressman and incoming Florida governor, said that 2028 hopefuls will need to redefine their own coalitions and not recreate the previous administrations. “To be blunt: What I’ve observed in politics, it’s very hard for somebody to try to recreate the previous person’s coalition,” Donalds told Politico at the National Governors Association’s New Governors Leadership Forum in part on Thursday. Donalds made history as Florida's first Black governor to be elected to office. President Donald Trump threw his support behind Donalds as did Florida Governor Ron DeSantis after the primary. Following devastating midterm election losses for Republicans, which resulted in losing both House and Senate majority, speculation has swirled surrounding who will be the successor to MAGA after Trump is out of office. DeSantis' post-midterm media rounds have sparked intrigue into whether he is considering another bid for the White House. He was asked about a potential 2028 run by CNN's Jake Tapper after Election Day and said in part that he has not "planned anything." Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, Glenn Youngkin, former Republican governor of Virginia, and many more have all been asked about their intentions for running in 2028 on the Republican side. Similarly, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and many more have also been asked about their political futures on the Democratic side. What To Know During his conversation with Politico's Adam Wren, Donalds said that “Whoever the next person is going to be, they’re going to have to — in some respects — redefine and reshape the electorate about what their supportive coalition is.“ "I think trying to go back into trying to recreate what somebody else’s success was, I think is foolhardy,” he added. Donalds was asked by Politico if his comments were aimed at Vance, and he responded in part that it is "just the reality of politics,” and running on someone else's coalition "rarely works." “I would advise anybody who’s thinking about taking the next step: You got to define yourself,” Donalds also told the outlet on Thursday. “You have to be yourself. You can’t be a facsimile or a carbon copy or shades of gray of somebody else.” Following the midterm losses, Trump administration officials speculated on why the results unfolded in such a bruising manner. Vance said that after speaking with a pollster, four areas jumped out, including ending the war with Iran, focusing on the cost of living and inflation, putting America first and changing America's relationship with Israel. Trump was asked if he had spoken with Vance about 2028 after the midterms and said in part earlier this month, "We'll see what happens. ... You don't know who's talking about running. ... Maybe he won't run, I don't know who's gonna run." Last month, Vance said he thought the president would endorse him should he launch an official 2028 campaign but added they had not discussed it. Donalds also shot down any potential 2028 run for himself saying to Politico that he is "absolutely" shutting the door on it, adding "it is not happening." “I take this job very seriously,” he later added. “I am not looking at another one.” Craig Agranoff, political professor at Florida Atlantic University, told Newsweek on Thursday, "Donalds is saying the obvious out loud. Coalitions are personal. Trump’s is built around him. [Former President Barack] Obama’s was built around him. Trying to photocopy either one usually fails. The next Republican nominee will have to assemble something that fits their own strengths and the electorate of 2028, not 2024. That is basic politics, not a break with Trump. "His quick no on running himself is also practical. He just won Florida. He has a full term ahead, a legislature to manage, and a record to build. Jumping into a national primary before he has governed would look premature to most voters and donors," Agranoff added. "It keeps the focus on the job he just got and leaves the 2028 field open for others who are already positioning. It is the kind of clear answer that avoids speculation without creating new problems." What Prediction Markets Show On prediction market Kalshi Thursday night, Vance has a 33 percent chance of winning the GOP presidential nomination. Rubio has 22 percent and DeSantis has 16 percent. On Polymarket, Vance has 33 percent Thursday night, Rubio has 21 percent, DeSantis has 15 percent and other potential candidates, including Cruz, Youngkin and Republican Congressman Thomas Massie of Kentucky, all have single digits. news.title: New PAC launches effort to recruit Pete Buttigieg for president in 2028
news.text:
Pete Buttigieg has not said whether he will run for president in 2028. But a new political action committee is not waiting for an announcement and has started a drive to draft the former transportation secretary as a contender.

Team Pete Pac, a volunteer-led progressive group that launched Wednesday, is working to ramp up excitement for Buttigieg ahead of the 2028 election. The organization, led by many of his former staffers, is unaffiliated with Buttigieg, who has not confirmed whether he will seek the Oval Office. “I doubt that I will be the first to make news,” Buttigieg said about the prospect of a presidential bid on MS NOW’s “Morning Joe” on Wednesday, adding that he is “certainly not cooking up anything to announce in the next few weeks.”While the possibility of his running is “no secret,” he said, “there’s no rush when you’re thinking about something of that weight.” 

Mohsin Syed, Buttigieg’s former chief of staff at the Transportation Department, is one of the PAC’s founders, along with Jennifer Holdsworth, a Democratic strategist who managed Buttigieg’s 2017 campaign for chair of the Democratic National Committee before he dropped out of the race.

“Jennifer and I have worked closely with Pete in different stages of his career, and have seen firsthand his inspirational leadership and clarity of purpose," Syed told MS NOW. "Along with so many supporters, we are eager to see Pete bring that leadership to the presidency and want to demonstrate his commitment to community service in the meantime.”Buttigieg is among several being eyed as potential Democratic presidential candidates in what is expected to be a crowded field in 2028.

A similar effort, Ready for AOC, launched earlier this month to encourage Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., to announce a presidential campaign. The progressive, widely seen as a potential successor to the political movement ignited by independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, has not ruled out a run but has stopped short of giving a definitive answer.

“I think, right now, this election just happened. We’ve got to work on getting results for people,” Ocasio-Cortez told Fox News on Tuesday when asked whether she was considering a bid in 2028, adding that she “is less about the horse race.”

Rep. Ro Khanna, a progressive Democrat from California, told MS NOW earlier this month that he is “strongly considering” a campaign, after his supporters launched Run Ro, a similar PAC, which it says is not affiliated with Khanna.Other potential Democratic candidates include California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris. None have formally declared an intent to run.So far, Vice President JD Vance appears to be the main Republican contender, but has not formally announced any plans. Vance said he will make a decision about the election “sometime next year.”

Buttigieg, once so inspired by Sanders’ progressive politics that he wrote an award-winning essay in high school about the lawmaker, has in more recent years moved toward the center on prominent policy issues, including U.S. support for Israel, universal healthcare and the student loan debt crisis.He split with his party on student loans, a key plank of former President Joe Biden’s 2024 campaign, telling “Pod Save America” last week that he struggles to explain to his relatives in Michigan who did not attend college why they should help pay the debt for those who did.“I believe there are ways to make sure that you come out of college debt-free. I believe college should be more affordable,” he said. “I don’t believe in like a magic wand to fix that for everybody who borrowed money.”If he runs, it would be his second attempt at the nation’s highest office. If elected, Buttigieg would be the country’s first openly gay president.

news.title: Emerson: Guess Who Moved Up in 2028 Sweepstakes After the Midterms?
news.text:
Too soon? Well ... it's not as early as people assume. As I wrote on Tuesday, presidential-candidacy announcements – at least for "exploratory committees" – routinely take place in the same month as the midterms that precede them. The field is usually known before New Year's Eve, with January being a straggler month for the last couple of decades.

In other words, there is no rest for the wicked. Not in this century, anyway.

With that in mind, get ready for the pollsters and their amusing takes on the political environment for the 2028 cycle. That has already started, too, as four pollsters have published surveys for the open primaries coming in both parties. Emerson College has a new result today that shows a big shift in pre-midterm polling on the GOP primary race:

In the open-ended Republican Primary, 36% named Marco Rubio, 20% JD Vance, 7% Ron DeSantis, 7% current President Donald Trump, and 7% Thomas Massie. In the closed-ended question, 44% support Marco Rubio, 24% JD Vance, 9% Ron DeSantis, and 6% Donald Trump Jr. When asked about the two major political parties, a majority have an unfavorable view of the Republican Party (56%), while 35% have a favorable view of it. The Democratic Party is also underwater by three points, 47% unfavorable to 44% favorable. Democrats’ favorable rating increased nine points in the past year. Republicans’ favorable rating decreased nine points, and their unfavorable rating increased 12 points to majority unfavorable at 56%.

Prior to the midterms, Vance led the field by a significant amount. Since the midterms, RCP's aggregate average now has Rubio up by less than two points over Vance, although that may have a boost from a pre-Election Week poll from Atlas Intel that had Rubio up thirteen points. Rubio's ascent may have something to do with Vance's attempt to distance himself from Trump and Israel two weeks ago, which at least correlates to Vance being out in public much less than previously scheduled. 

Still, the horse-race aspect is a little premature, even for a curtain-raiser. Rather than delve into the particulars, it's better to look at the pattern emerging in polling for both primaries. In all five polls in RCP's aggregate, support has coalesced around three candidates: Rubio, Vance, and DeSantis, all of whom have double-digit averages for support. Everyone else polled has numbers that fall below the margins of error for most polls. There may be new entrants that could disturb that coalescence, such as Sarah Huckabee Sanders, but right now, 80 percent of Republicans polled on 2028 have chosen one of the three. (If Vance chooses to stay out, that would open up more possibilities, of course.)

What about Democrats? The most notable pattern here is that no one's moving up. 

RCP's aggregation of four polls for their upcoming presidential primary over the past month shows a much broader distribution of support. Where Rubio and Vance average around 35 percent each in polling, not one Democrat polls any higher than 16.5 percent, Kamala Harris' aggregate average. Harris has barely led two of these polls and tied in another, but Jon Ossoff edged Harris in Emerson's survey without either of them moving much at all:

In the open-ended Democratic Primary, Jon Ossoff (17%) and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (12%) top the list of candidates, followed by Gavin Newsom (8%), Pete Buttigieg (6%), Kamala Harris (6%), Andy Beshear (4%), and Mark Kelly (3%). In the closed-ended question, 17% support Ossoff, 16% Kamala Harris, 15% AOC, 14% Pete Buttigieg, 11% Gavin Newsom, 7% Andy Beshear, 4% Mark Kelly, and 3% Josh Shapiro and JB Pritzker, respectively.

Jon Ossoff? How did Ossoff get ahead of Democrat governors like Newsom, Beshear, Shapiro, and Pritzker? For that matter, how did he get ahead of AOC? The answer is that he really hasn't. What we're seeing so far across these four polls is a two-tier field that has five candidates in a virtual tie with around 70 percent of Democrat voters, and 30 percent more inclined to the second tier. 

What can we take away from these patterns? Republicans seem to have a clearer idea of what should follow this final Trump term than Democrats do. news.title: Tech Billionaires Really Do Think We’re All Idiots, Don’t They?
news.text:
One week after the blue wave swept at the midterm elections, Palantir CEO Alex Karp announced that he was actually super liberal. Possibly the best liberal that you have ever seen. Certainly a better liberal than you.

“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life,” he said in an interview with Politico. “I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”

He isn’t the only billionaire who’s seemed to change his mind. Elon Musk, who is most famous for aligning himself with far-right politicians and also Looking Like That, and who spent $277 million on Donald Trump’s campaign and $474 million to try to stop Democratic Sen. James Talarico from getting into office, logged onto a video call at a New York Times summit this week and said the following words: “I’m not MAGA.” Yes, the guy who maybe Nazi-saluted, the guy who called himself “dark MAGA” last year, the guy who hit the High School Musical jump at a Trump rally is not—not!—a Republican. You’re the one with that silly idea!

“I’m not sure what MAGA means,” Musk said. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

Meta has also tried to go purple, deepening ties with Democratic Washington veterans during the week of the election after CEO Mark Zuckerberg spent so long cozying up to the Trump administration. (Here’s some photos of them laughing and smiling and leaning their foreheads into each other.) Microsoft and Apple have also hired Democratic lobbyists to brace for the inevitable probing and questioning that they face after so flagrantly and openly playing in voters’ faces for the past four years as they so belligerently played a role in the politics that impacted everyone’s lives. Big Tech is hitting Uno reverse on the past two years—but I have some questions about what, besides their proximity to the people signing the checks, these billionaires actually intend to change.

Take Karp, whose progressive credentials appear to include everything other than what he does to make his money. One could make an argument that Karp could be considered liberal, in some twisted sense of the word. There’s evidence to support this. In 2015, he was caught on tape criticizing Trump in a Palantir staff meeting, saying, “I respect nothing about the dude” and that “it would be hard to make up someone that I find less appealing.” He publicly backed Kamala Harris’ campaign in 2024. There’s a picture of him wearing a keffiyeh in his college yearbook that sometimes gets circulated like an urban myth (Palantir posted in support of Israel in 2024). Sure, some could make the argument that Karp is liberal, perhaps, in the same way that putting a Coexist sticker on the back of a Cadillac Escalade is liberal, or wearing Temu pussy hats in this day and age could be considered liberal, or putting “moderate” in your Hinge profile can be convincing as potentially liberal if you turn off all the lights and squint. Throw a rock in any major American city and you will hit someone working for an A.I. defense startup who wants to claim the same political affiliation, simply because they’ve read Marx and Engels before.

It’s easy to make fun of these statements because any claims of leftism are quickly eclipsed by the human impact that these corporations have had on people living in the country. Zuckerberg also started off criticizing Trump’s first term, and the two have feuded as Trump threatened to ban Facebook, but years later, they’re getting dinner together, and Zuckerberg’s shaping A.I. policy in this country.

Palantir’s public positioning is not unlike Karp’s politics. The company is officially known for its management, data analysis, and visualization software. Its workers have called themselves digital “plumbers,” joining leaky or disconnected pipes of information together with A.I. tools so scattered datasets can be analyzed with ease. But much of its internal work has remained largely shielded from the public, which the company claims is for client confidentiality.

Here’s what we know: A bunch of smaller companies have user data—shopping habits, demographics, the random subscriptions that are pooling in inboxes, everyone’s geolocations used for picking up food or reselling furniture or whatever. Palantir aggregates all of this, and then helps its clients access these different databases, synthesizing all this scattered information into one clean channel of analysis for whatever purpose. They can help a marketing company figure out at what price point you’re most likely to buy their products, based on your abandoned shopping carts across all your favorite stores. They can also help ICE figure out when you’re most likely to be at home or at work or at church, so they know how to pick where to raid. (Palantir denies that they are making predictive policing tools, although arrests have been made in cities across America with Palantir-partnered predictive policing tools.)

This is the cultural switch-up that Palantir constantly plays: They have established a reputation as being mysterious and all-powerful, because they have all our data, but then people involved with the company have spent an astounding amount of airtime trying to shirk accountability around the impact of their work, or worse, not being able to articulate what it is they do at all. They know everything, and also nothing. Alex Karp and co-founder Peter Thiel have denied that Palantir ushered in an era of predictive policing, overreaching government surveillance, and mining sensitive user data, although the bulk of their public-facing partnerships are with the military and police forces, as well as private defense corporations like Anduril and Lockheed Martin, so all the arrows kind of point in one direction. Karp claims he is actually progressive, so how could someone who grew up in a “far-left” environment with granola and stuff possibly be manufacturing a back-end national surveillance dataset and selling it to the military?

To be clear, what Karp actually politically identifies as is a sycophant. His financial donations have been scattered between Republicans and Democrats alike, and he’s spent most of his time in politics aggressively glazing whatever party in power holds the coin purse that re-signs the Department of Defense contracts with Palantir. It’s a level of dick-riding that many might not have believed possible: In December 2024, just one month after Kamala Harris lost the election that Karp himself endorsed her in, he got on stage and started dunking on Democrats for their “woke pagan ideology”; the next year, he said that any claims that Trump is a fascist are “stupid” and “idiotic” in a panel with the New York Times. Earlier this year, he also published an “anti-woke” manifesto in a 22-part Twitter thread that sparked huge amounts of discourse. No one throws it back like Karp does.

Getting involved in politics is not part of his job description, but it has worked out. Karp has won the company hundreds of millions of dollars under the Trump administration. Palantir has played a pivotal role in the president’s mass deportation campaign and widespread policing across this country. And for all these jovial lamentations that Karp thinks Trump went “too far” in the violent detainment of immigrants and citizens alike, Palantir still has a $377 billion market cap.

I do not think all hope is lost, though. I think there is a bulletproof solution to Karp’s desire to pivot left. This is a solution for any tech billionaire looking to convince the public that they’re actually, seriously—no, seriously—progressive: Give me all the money.

All the money you have.

Give it away, and give it to me.

Give it to schools to buy free school lunches and hospitals to pay off medical debt and libraries for lots of smutty romance books.

Give it to Cardi B, who can set up funds for people to get food assistance and all-expenses-paid girls’ trips to Miami or something for overworked women and also women who are going through breakups.

And mostly, give it to me. I have a bunch of stuff I want to buy, including paying down my friends’ student loans and medical debt and then also getting some matching shoes.

My demands do not end there. Once you give me the money, dissolve Palantir and dye your hair blue for good measure, and start experimenting with your pronouns. If you’re really about the superprogressive leftist life, start arguing with your co-organizers in a shared Google Doc about logistics for the upcoming local government sit-in. I think that would be very progressive. I think if you all did that, I would say, “Wow, Alex Karp knows more about being progressive than anyone on the planet.” (No, I still probably wouldn’t say that, because what’s past is prologue. But I’d be far more likely to say that.)

Until then, no dice! Alex Karp and associates want to glaze Democratic senators for taxpayer money without giving anything first. That’s my money and your money that they’re currently prancing around on podcasts for. The smallest sin that Karp has to pay for is the fact that Palantir is possibly the most criminally incorrect LARP of Lord of the Rings in history (the company, named after the series’ omnipresent “seeing stone,” has been dragged online for the fact that the entire moral of J.R.R. Tolkien’s Palantír was that it was an unreliable guide, calling into question if these tech bros have critical thinking abilities), and those restitutions are already starting at a pretty steep price. As more tech billionaires have to figure out how to align themselves with a Democratic-majority Congress, I expect direct deposits in the process. There’s no other way out. If they really want to be the best liberals we’ve ever seen.
news.summary: Tech billionaires are rediscovering their liberal credentials. I have a modest proposal for making them prove it.

news.title: JD Vance behind Marco Rubio as top choice for Republicans in 2028 poll
news.text:
WASHINGTON − Vice President JD Vance has slipped as the top choice of Republican voters in the 2028, race for president, according to a new national poll from Emerson College.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is the top choice for Republicans and Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff has surged ahead in the early field of potential Democratic presidential candidates,

The poll, released Nov. 19, found 36% of Republican primary voters prefer Rubio as the 2028 Republican nominee, followed by Vance, who is the top choice of 20%. It marks a complete turnabout from a year ago, when the same pollster had Vance ahead of Rubio by a whopping 54%-6%.

Rounding out the poll of Republican 2028 contenders are Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, President Donald Trump (who is barred under the Constitution from seeking a third term), and Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, a Trump critic who lost his primary reelection this year. Each are backed by 7% of Republicans as the party's nominee.

More: The race for 2028 is on as Republicans unpack midterm disaster

In the 2028 Democratic contest, the Emerson poll found Ossoff the top choice of 17% of self-identified Democratic primary voters, followed by New York Rep Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 12%; California Gov. Gavin Newsom, 8%; former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, 6%; former Vice President Kamala Harris, 6%; Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, 4%; and Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, 3%.

Ossoff catapults among Democrats fresh off midterm glow

For Ossoff, his rapid rise comes after attracting the national spotlight in the 2026 midterm campaign, which was capped by winning reelection in Georgia by 18 percentage points in a blue tsunami for Democrats. Ossoff did not register any support in the Emerson presidential poll taken in 2025.

On the campaign trail, Ossoff said repeatedly that he's not interested in running for president in 2028. Georgia's other Democratic senator, Raphael Warnock, is also considered a potential 2028 Democratic contender.

More: Trump says he may not endorse in 2028 Republican presidential primary

On the Republican side, polls for months have shown Vance gradually ceding ground to Rubio. A Reuters/Ipsos poll last week also found Rubio leading Vance and other Republicans, with Ossoff in first place among Democrats.

Vance's fall from the top spot follows a devastating midterm election for Republicans that was widely interpreted as a repudiation of the Trump administration and the war in Iran. Vance publicly blamed the war in Iran for Republicans' midterm losses. Trump later pulled Vance off leading negotiations with Iran, arguing that a deal with Tehran is not needed.

Trump surprised many observers this month by saying he may not endorse anyone in the 2028 Republican primary. It's long been widely assumed that Trump would try to anoint who replaces him.

The Emerson poll, conducted online and via text messages Nov. 14-16, is based on a sample of 1,000 registered voters nationally − 499 of whom said they planned to vote in the 2028 Democratic primary, and 418 who are planning to vote in the Republican primary. The poll has a margin of error of plus or minus three percentage points.

Regarding 2028 preferences, respondents were asked an open-ended question that did not provide options. Rubio's support increased to 44% and Vance's to 24% when respondents were asked a follow-up question that identified a list of candidates from which to choose.

When Democratic primary voters were given a list of potential 2028 candidates, Ossoff's support remained at 17%, tops among Democratic candidates. Ossoff was followed by Harris, 16%; Ocasio-Cortez, 15%; Buttigieg, 11%; Newsom, 7%; Beshear, 7%; and Kelly, 4%. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker each had 3%.

news.text:
Greetings, and welcome to Thursday, November 19, 2026. 

My calendar says it's National Play Monopoly Day, National Carbonated Beverage With Caffeine Day, Have a Bad Day Day, and the Great American Smokeout. Dust off the Monopoly board tonight. Consider it a warm-up for the family arguments at the Thanksgiving table next week. Crack open a cold cola to keep you sharp while you're buying Boardwalk. If someone at the checkout tells you to have a nice day, go ahead and tell them to have a bad one; today, it's practically a courtesy. And if you smoke, take the day off from the habit. Your lungs will thank you, and so will whoever sits across the Monopoly board.

Today in History:1794: The United States and Britain sign the Jay Treaty, settling disputes left over from the Revolutionary War.1863: President Abraham Lincoln delivers the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery in Pennsylvania.1959: Ford Motor Co. announces it will discontinue the Edsel, one of the most famous flops in automotive history.1969: Apollo 12 astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean land on the moon's Ocean of Storms, the second crewed lunar landing.1969: Brazilian soccer star Pelé scores the 1,000th goal of his career on a penalty kick at Rio de Janeiro's Maracanã Stadium.1977: Egyptian President Anwar Sadat becomes the first Arab leader to make an official visit to Israel.1985: President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev meet for the first time, at a summit in Geneva.1990: Milli Vanilli is stripped of its Grammy for best new artist after admitting the duo never sang on its album.1998: The House Judiciary Committee opens impeachment hearings against President Bill Clinton.

Birthdays Today include: James A. Garfield, the 20th president of the United States; Billy Sunday, the ballplayer turned fire-and-brimstone evangelist; Tommy Dorsey, big-band trombonist and bandleader; Indira Gandhi, India's first female prime minister; Roy Campanella, Hall of Fame catcher for the Brooklyn Dodgers; Larry King, host of Larry King Live; Ted Turner, founder of CNN; Calvin Klein, fashion designer; Meg Ryan, actress from When Harry Met Sally; and Jodie Foster, actress from The Silence of the Lambs. If today's your birthday, too, happy birthday from all of us here.

It’s become one of the more widely recognized axioms of this column that this country has two problems: The Democrat party and the establishment Republicans. Of the two, the axiom holds the establishment GOP to be the more treacherous, because at least the Democrats aren’t trying to pass themselves off as Republicans, and certainly not conservatives, as the establishment GOP is.

I’ve written repeatedly on the history of the establishment GOP, most recently here, where I drilled a new hole with my oversized corkscrew in the hindquarters of publications like The Bulwark. And of course, specifically, Bill Kristol. I’ve also suggested that the establishment GOP will use recent events in an attempt to reestablish and rehab itself into something resembling a political power.

So it was no shock to find that one of the establishment critters, Jonah Goldberg, has popped up on the horizon again, trying to do just that. Ed Driscoll over at Instapundit noted it last night. I won’t bother quote-blocking Ed’s post. (Ed has been known to use rather extended quotes to make his points, and I like to keep this daily column a bit shorter where I can.) Instead, I’ll send you to this link to get the feel of it.

It’s not an accident that Goldberg surfaces before the echo of the most recent election has died. I said the RINOs were going to try and reassert themselves, and here comes Goldberg, right on cue. 

Recommended: Nigeria Challenges Climate Dogma and Revives Gas Project

Consider what he’s been up to. In the two weeks since the votes were counted, Goldberg has been filing at a pace that would make a wire-service stringer blush. The Friday after the election, his G-File ran under the headline “I Was Right About the New Right,” subhead: “The GOP got the drubbing it deserved.” Next came “The New Right Can’t Run Away From Trump,” which accuses Oren Cass of blaming the Reaganites for problems the populists made themselves. (Intentionally forgetting, of course, that Reagan himself was largely a populist, which is why the establishment spent most of the next four decades trying to expunge him from the party memory). 

Then a piece telling conservatives the midterms carry a silver lining because red-state Democrats won by running to the right. And yesterday came the main event: “Why I Squabbled With The Bulwark.”

Look at the order. "I told you so." Second, "it’s the populists’ fault." Third, "here’s the lesson the party should take." Fourth, some careful distance from the people who embarrassed the Never Trump brand.

I'm getting tired of pretending I don't notice the pattern, so I'm just going to say this out loud: That isn’t a man processing an election defeat. That’s a squish, trying desperately to reposition himself as a conservative while adopting none of the character traits of an actual conservative.

The squabble between Goldberg and The Bulwark, et al., itself is instructive. It started when Bulwark publisher Sarah Longwell told a Democrat gathering in Colorado, “We’re just kind of libs, just like the rest of you.” Credit where due: Goldberg called that spin. He pointed out that the outfit founded to preserve conservatism saw Bill Kristol, once a pro-life Republican, backing Kamala Harris, and backing Zohran Mamdani over Andrew Cuomo for good measure. Regular readers will recognize this as the point I made on October 29, when I called The Bulwark “a Democratic outlet with a Rolodex full of ex-GOP staffers.” Sam Stein’s own subscription pitch all but said so.

So why does Goldberg care now? Because the Bulwark crowd said the quiet part out loud. That’s a problem for anyone hoping to sell the old establishment as the “adult” option once Trump is gone. He sees the Never Trump brand as damaged and is building a firewall between the faction that openly went over to the Democrats and the faction that hopes to be invited back to the table. He wants to be the "respectable" one. He's assessed the damage more or less correctly, but he's also beginning to understand the wall between himself and the Bulwark crowd to be vanishingly thin. 

How do I know? Well, look at what he concedes along the way. He says he largely agrees (incorrectly) with The Bulwark about the danger Trump poses. He says he isn’t particularly proud to be a Republican and votes for the party mostly because that’s where conservatives happen to live. Fine. Almost honest, even. Almost. But it means the difference between Goldberg and Kristol was never where they stood on the man Republican voters nominated three times. It’s only how far each was willing to walk once he got there. Kristol walked all the way to the Democrats. Goldberg stopped at the edge of the parking lot, and he would now like credit for not getting in the car.

We’ve seen this movie before. The establishment never accepted Reagan, either. See, Reagan didn't simply win elections; he changed what the Republican Party was supposed to stand for. The establishment spent years trying to erase that change, rather than embrace it. George H.W. Bush dismissed Reagan’s agenda as “voodoo economics” in the 1980 primaries, rode Reagan’s coattails into the White House, and then, in 1990, cut the budget deal that broke his “Read my lips: no new taxes” pledge. The voters remembered in 1992. After that came Dole, McCain, and Romney. Every time, the pitch was the same: The grownups are back in charge. Every time, a large part of the base stayed home. (I went through that whole sorry history in “The Usual Suspects”.)

That’s why the timing matters. The window for a rehab job is right now, while the party is licking its wounds and before the 2028 field takes shape. Donors are asking what went wrong. Cable bookers want a “reasonable conservative” who will tell the audience the problem was Trump. And the voters who keep choosing him. Whoever gets to define the loss gets to define what comes next. Goldberg knows that, and so does everyone else in the establishment who has been waiting out the populists the way they once tried to wait out Reagan. He wants to be the left's favorite Republican in much the same way John McCain was. Lots of money in those TV appearances, ya know.

So here’s a reminder for those of us who actually vote in Republican primaries. When someone who has spent a decade explaining why the voters were wrong shows up to explain what the voters really meant, check your wallet. The establishment’s strategy has always been patience. Ours has to be memory.

Thought for the day: On this date in 1863, Lincoln gave the Gettysburg Address. He spoke for about two minutes and told the crowd, “The world will little note, nor long remember what we say here.” He was wrong about that. You see, the words that last are rarely the ones written for the purpose of being remembered. They’re the ones written because something needed saying.

Take care of yourselves today, Gang. I'll see you here tomorrow.

news.title: ASRA Q. NOMANI: Old-guard Dems face Frankenstein moment as leftists come for them
news.text: WASHINGTON, D.C. — Ice cream magnate Ben Cohen and activists from the far-left nonprofit CodePink packed into a lawmaker's office in House Longworth Building Room 1236 last week, demanding an end to the war in Iran, a cutoff of U.S. military ties to Israel and the removal of Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth. Next door, in House Rayburn Building Room 2267, Capitol police officers arrested far-left, anti-Israel demonstrators, including prolific street theater activist Hazami Barmada, cloaked in symbolic blood red, as they packed another lawmaker's office, condemning complicity in Israel's alleged "genocide" of Palestinians in Gaza. Across Capitol Hill in Senate Hart Building Room 322, police officers arrested young adults from a far-left nonprofit and political action committee, Sunrise Movement, as they packed a senator's office, condemning his politics, including his support of Israel. The next day, an activist from a far-left nonprofit, Climate Defiance, screamed at a high-ranking lawmaker speaking at a political conference, calling him a "traitor." But they weren't going after Republican lawmakers. They were far-left activists with a special target: The Democratic Party's leadership. JEFFRIES BRUSHES OFF OPPOSITION FROM FAR-LEFT DEMS WHO VOTED NO: 'WE’RE GOING TO WORK TOGETHER' The target of Cohen, the co-founder of Ben and Jerry's, was California Democratic Rep. Nancy Pelosi, former speaker of the House. The anti-Israel protesters had filled the office of Democratic Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, nominated Wednesday by fellow Democrats to be the next House speaker despite the protests. The Sunrise Movement agitators had flooded the office of top Senate Democrat Chuck Schumer, and the activists of Climate Defiance were attempting to shame Jeffries at a conference of the Democratic Party. The groups protesting top Democrats represent the full spectrum of a "red-green-green-blue" alliance – made up of socialist and pro-communist "red" organizations, Muslim and Arab "green" groups, environmental "green" activists and traditional "blue" groups. The alliance has emerged in recent years to press a far-left agenda in U.S. politics, particularly on the issue of ending U.S. support for Israel. A Fox News Digital investigation reveals that 22 groups from the network – harnessing about $342 million in annual revenues – are now waging a coordinated effort, dubbed "CHUCK CHUCK," aimed at ousting Schumer from his expected role as Senate majority leader, creating the myth of the marching millions with shared messaging, social media campaigns, influencer videos and staged arrests. The campaign is operating on several fronts: activists "bird-dogging" lawmakers in the halls of Congress, national advocacy organizations endorsing Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen over Schumer, local chapters organizing demonstrations and supporters mobilizing phone calls to senators ahead of a Dec. 1 secret-ballot leadership election. On Monday, Brooklyn activists from a traditionally Democratic group, Indivisible Project, plan to "celebrate" Schumer's 76th birthday with a protest against him at his Third Avenue midtown Manhattan office. Schumer maintains that he has the votes to win, and he most likely does. A Fox News Digital anti-Schumer tracker shows that Van Hollen only has the support of five sitting or incoming senators: Bernie Sanders, Abdul El-Sayed, Jeff Merkley, Peggy Flanagan and himself. But he does have 22 organizations fueling and amplifying the anti-Schumer campaign to win more votes. So far, they include: SCHUMER BOASTS EARLY ADVANTAGE IN SENATE POWER STRUGGLE AS DEM RIVAL WARNS AGAINST 'CORONATION' The emerging dynamics are reminiscent of the Frankenstein story, with the Democratic establishment empowering the powerful activist movement to defeat its Republican opponents. But now, parts of that movement are turning on the very political establishment that helped bring them to power. Earlier this year, the Sunrise Movement's executive director, Aru Shiney-Ajay, led an online discussion, published on YouTube, headlined "How to Take Over the Democratic Party." Neera Tanden, a longtime ally of Bill and Hillary Clinton and now executive director of the Center for American Progress, a Democratic nonprofit created by former Clinton administration chief of staff John Podesta, has another term for the rebels from within who challenge Jeffries: "chaos agents." On Tuesday, she wrote on X, "I personally would like the names of everyone who wins an historic election and then immediately goes into a circular firing squad so we can tag the chaos agents for the future." Meanwhile, witnessing the targeting of Jeffries as a "traitor," Texas Democratic Party advisor Kurt Bardella wrote on X, "I can tell you there are times when the tactics and venom coming from the activist left are completely indistinguishable to the MAGA right. They just come off as unhinged a--holes who are throwing tantrums." PROGRESSIVES FACE ACCUSATIONS OF RACISM OVER ATTACKS ON HAKEEM JEFFRIES AS HE SEEKS SPEAKERSHIP When Code Pink co-founder Medea Benjamin emerged from Pelosi's office last week, trailing behind Capitol Police officers called by staffers to assess the situation, she told Fox News Digital: "See, we're bipartisan. We yell at Democrats as much as we yell and scream at Republicans." Importantly, for some of them, the goal of the "red" in the red-green-green-blue alliance isn't Western free-enterprise democracy. Benjamin's fellow CodePink co-founder, Jodie Evans, gave Fox News Digital a more ideological explanation for rejecting Democrats alongside Republicans, as she stood outside Pelosi's office. "I'm a socialist, because I believe in equality, so I teach it. It's the peace economy," Evans said. "Socialism is the peace of economy. I read Marx to try to understand why we were at war with communists. Like, well, how bad were they?... They wanted equality for everyone! What insanity!" The encounters last week captured a fault line running through the opposition to President Donald Trump. Some activists want to push the Democratic Party further left. Others who are openly pro-socialist and pro-communist reject both major parties and see a Democratic victory as another opportunity to organize against the political establishment. QUIET PART OUT LOUD: ANTI-ISRAEL MOBS WANT ONE STATE CALLED 'PALESTINE,' ERASING ISRAEL Most importantly, a connective thread runs through the protests by the "red-green-green-blue" alliance: anti-Israel messaging. Within the broader pro-Palestinian movement, activists advocate different goals, including a Palestinian "right of return" to Israel, a single democratic "one state" encompassing Israel and the Palestinian territories, an end to "Zionism" and Israel's status as a Jewish state, and the emergence of a "free, free Palestine" "from the river to the sea." Proponents of a "one-state" solution argue that Palestinians and their descendants displaced following Israel's creation in 1948 should be permitted the "right of return" and receive "equal rights" in Israel. Critics contend that such a demographic transformation would end Israel's character as a Jewish homeland. Supporters invoke "rules-based international law" to describe their proposals as a framework for "human rights," "equal rights" and "self-determination" for Palestinians. These fissures with centrist Democrats are being expressed by the leaders of groups including CodePink, BreakThrough BT Media, the People's Forum and Tricontinental, funded by American-born communist tycoon Neville Roy Singham, who lives in Shanghai, supporting the Chinese Communist Party. CodePink's Evans is married to Singham. Congressional investigators and Justice Department prosecutors have investigated Singham's activities and funding as possible malign foreign influence. No charges have been filed against Singham or the groups he has funded. SCHUMER'S LEADERSHIP RIVAL REVEALS MAJOR SENATE RULE CHANGE HE'D PURSUE IF ELECTED Even with Jeffries' leadership survival, their targets include the two Democrats positioned to lead the incoming congressional Democratic majority – Schumer and Jeffries – with disputes over U.S. support for Israel among the grievances raised by activists interviewed by Fox News Digital. The confrontations harken back to the protests surrounding the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, where demonstrators gathered at Union Park and marched toward the convention, denouncing Vice President Kamala Harris as "Killer Kamala" and President Joe Biden as "Genocide Joe" for supporting Israel in its campaign against Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel. Some of the same organizations and activists challenging Democrats today were gathered in Union Park back then. Two years later, Democrats’ midterm victories have brought another round of demands, demonstrations and threats to withhold support from Democratic Party leaders. In an April 2025 interview with New York magazine, Alexander Soros, son of billionaire Democratic Party funder George Soros, expressed his frustration with the leftist environmentalist group Sunrise Movement, which has been heavily funded by Soros organizations. "What the hell did they do, by the way?" Soros said in the interview. "We gave them money, and now all they do is talk about Palestine. It’s ridiculous." ALEX SOROS FUMES AT LEFT-WING CLIMATE GROUP OVER 'PALESTINE' OBSESSION The dynamics of the "chaos agents" ramped up even as votes were still being counted from the Democratic Party's "blue tsunami" wins in the midterm elections. On Nov. 4, the day after the election, BreakThrough News host Rania Khalek, in D.C. last week for lobbying organized by CodePink, led a panel discussion with co-host Zoe Alexandra featuring the top Singham network personalities — BreakThrough News editor-in-chief Ben Becker; People's Forum executive director Manolo De Los Santos; and Tricontinental executive director Vijay Prashad — blasting the Democrats. That day, the Democratic Socialists of America declared that voters had "emphatically endorsed socialism" and urged Americans to reject "the complacent center and the fascist right." The next day, BreakThrough published a Khalek segment titled "Schumer & Jeffries reap the backlash to the genocide they enabled," accusing the Democratic leaders of benefiting politically from opposition to policies they had helped sustain. Khalek followed the next day with a written appeal linking to her "BT Live" segment. She accused Democratic leaders of serving wealthy interests and argued that sustained organizing could force policy concessions. "Do not go back to brunch. Get organized," she wrote. Also on Nov. 5, Our Revolution, a 501(c)(4) political nonprofit backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, an elder statesman revered by members of the Democratic Socialists of America, made clear that its leadership challenge extended to both chambers. "Real question: how do people calling for Schumer to step down justify giving Hakeem Jeffries a pass?" the group posted. By Saturday, Nov. 7, that pressure was visible on Manhattan’s streets. Demonstrators marched from Times Square toward Seventh Avenue and 14th Street in a rally organized by groups including the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter. The protests were cast as anti-Trump but there was another theme in the crowd: anti-Democratic Party. Among their chants: "Jeffries, Schumer let’s be clear, ICE is not wanted here." Demonstrators held signs reading, "Remove Jeffries / Schumer" and "CALL JEFFRIES & SCHUMER / TELL THEM TO STEP ASIDE." One sign repeated the thread of anti-Israel activism, aimed also at the pro-Israel lobbying group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee: "They are not capable of meeting this moment. We need FIGHTERS with BACKBONE & VISION – not corporate & AIPAC hacks." By Sunday, Nov. 8, the Party for Socialism and Liberation, a communist group working out of the headquarters of the People's Forum on Wesr 37th Street in Manhattan, attacked Schumer directly. "Chuck Schumer isn’t an ‘architect’ of anything except the genocide in Gaza," the organization wrote, adding that Schumer had no place leading a Senate "which should be abolished anyway." CHAOS INC.: COMMUNISTS, ANTIFA, AGITATORS IN THE RED-GREEN ALLIANCE By early last week, the pressure campaign had reached Schumer’s and Jeffries' offices. At 12:51 p.m. on Tuesday, Nov. 10, CodePink's Benjamin tried to enter Schumer's office in Hart Room 322, and posted a video with the message: "Chuck Schumer locked his office on us!" The next day, at 10:35 a.m., the activists reached Jeffries' office in Rayburn Room 2267 and Benjamin recorded a staged statement outside the door for CodePink's social media account. On Thursday, Nov. 12, Barmada, wearing her red costume, joined a new confrontation at Jeffries’ office, filming as Capitol Police escorted other activists away. Iran's state-run Press TV later promoted the protest on its anti-U.S. propaganda platform. Barmada didn't respond to a request for comment. Across the Capitol complex, at 2:55 p.m., Schumer's staff faced the sit-in staged by Sunrise Movement's protest organizers, chanting on script, "Hey hey, ho ho, Schumer has got to go!" Capitol Police arrested 54 activists during the Sunrise Movement action, and a battalion of influencers splashed the news across social media in a series of similar posts. ASRA NOMANI: EL-SAYED GLIDES INTO ROLE AS ROCK STAR OF THE HARD LEFT'S RED-GREEN ALLIANCE By Thursday night, amid the coordinated campaign by the left, the campaign to replace Schumer had a declared candidate. Van Hollen announced he would seek the majority leader’s job, and El-Sayed endorsed him. Just days earlier, El-Sayed had smiled quietly as the board president of the Arab America Foundation led a supportive crowd in chants of "Free, free Palestine," "from the river to the sea." El-Sayed previously served on the board of the Sunrise Movement, whose organizers have been demanding Schumer's removal. The relationship illustrates how the pressure campaign extends beyond street demonstrations to elected Democrats with histories in activist organizations. That day, Democratic Socialists of America published a message, "SAY NO TO SCHUMER," over images of the leader. Soon after, the "World Socialist Web Site," representing a pro-communist "world Trotskyist movement" and "Marxist world outlook," promoted the "SAY NO TO SCHUMER" campaign, touting Van Hollen as a "lifelong servant of the Democratic establishment." The next day, CodePink's D.C. organizer, Olivia DiNucci, regularly seen heckling public officials and lawmakers, responded with a triumphant video, calling on activists to lobby against Schumer in the halls of Congress and flood congressional officials with the message: "VOTE CHRIS, NOT CHUCK." And, wearing a hot pink T-shirt with the graphic of a watermelon, a quirky symbol of Palestinian "resistance," and "Falasteen," the Arabic word for a Palestinian homeland, CodePink's Benjamin responded that day by urging support for Van Hollen, citing as her first reason: "He has been a forceful critic of Israel's assault on Palestinians." The campaign to oust Schumer is now drawing support from two of the Democratic Party’s most established "progressive" political nonprofits: Indivisible Project and MoveOn.org Civic Action, both 501(c)(4) nonprofits. Indivisible Project says it opposes Schumer's "coronation," and Indivisible Brooklyn is promoting an "Even New Yorkers Don’t Want Chuck" week of action, including a Times Square rally on Thursday, co-sponsored by other Indivisible chapters. MoveOn reports that 75% of participating members who voted support Van Hollen. Meanwhile, last Friday, Barmada posted a video with one of the activists arrested at Jeffries’ office. She wore a T-shirt that said, "FREE AMERICA FROM ISRAEL," with the image of an Israeli flag over the mouth of the Statue of Liberty. The back of her shirt read: "ISRAEL GETS BILLIONS / AMERICANS PAY THE BILL." She accused Jeffries of being "a mouthpiece for Israel, AIPAC, the Israeli lobby," and declared: "The Democrats are spineless." After the vote paving the way for Jeffries to become House speaker Wednesday, the activists in the red-green-green-blue alliance weren't relenting in their anti-Schumer campaign. At 2:05 p.m., the Council on American-Islamic Relations issued an "Action Alert" to support Van Hollen against "AIPAC's toxic influence over our politics." news.title: Independent, Gen Z and Latino voters helped deliver a Democratic wave in 2026 – but that doesn’t mean a lasting realignment
news.text:
The Democratic wave in the 2026 midterm elections raises an important question about American politics. Are independent, Gen Z and Latino voters building a new Democratic coalition, or are they sending a warning to both parties that their support cannot be taken for granted?

The preliminary evidence suggests something more complicated.

Our analysis, including a deep dive into the 2026 Voter Poll conducted by the market research firm SSRS, points to three factors behind the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories: a substantial shift among independent voters toward Democratic candidates, stronger Democratic turnout relative to Republicans, and declining enthusiasm among voters who supported Donald Trump in 2024. 

Gen Z, who are people born from 1997 to 2012, and Latino voters played important roles in these shifts.

But the results should not automatically be interpreted as a lasting Democratic realignment. These voters may be demonstrating a willingness to reconsider their political choices when governing parties fail to meet their expectations.

The overlapping influence of independent, younger and Latino voters helps explain the scale of the Democratic gains. Our analysis, based on voter poll data, suggests that independents, who made up about one-third of voters, contributed approximately 52% of the Democrats’ national popular vote margin in House races. Latino voters contributed an estimated 23% of that margin, while voters ages 18 to 29 contributed approximately 39%. 

Because these groups overlap, their contributions cannot be added together. But the figures illustrate how important each was to the Democratic advantage.

In our book, “The Independent Voter,” co-authored with Omar Ali, we examine the growing influence of independent voters and their often unpredictable voting behavior.

Independents helped determine the outcome

Independent voters, among the most important contributors to Democratic victories in the 2026 midterms, have repeatedly demonstrated a willingness to shift between parties.

In 2008, they favored Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama by 8 percentage points. Four years later, they backed Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney by 5 points. In the 2016 presidential election, independents favored Republican Trump by 4 points before swinging toward Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, supporting him by 13 points. 

In the 2024 presidential election, independents narrowly favored Democrat Kamala Harris over Trump, 49% to 46%. However, Trump performed better among independents in key battleground states, including Arizona, Georgia, Pennsylvania and North Carolina.

In our research spanning nearly five decades, Dan Hunting and I, Thom Reilly, found that independents exhibit considerably greater volatility in their voting patterns than Democrats and Republicans.

The 3-point advantage independents gave Harris in 2024 provides a useful baseline for understanding their much larger shift toward Democratic candidates in 2026. A November 2026 national survey of more than 90,000 people found that voters identifying with neither major party favored Democratic House candidates by more than 20 percentage points.

Our analysis of voter poll data showed that independents favored House Democrats by 59% to 37%. In addition, independents’ support was consequential in several Republican-held Senate seats that flipped to Democrats, with independent voters providing the margin needed for victory in six of the nine races: Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Mississippi, Ohio and South Carolina. 

The emerging pattern may represent another turn in a longer cycle of electoral volatility among independents. Rather than embracing either party, independent voters appear willing to reconsider their choices as political and economic conditions change.

Did Republicans switch sides or stay home?

There is some disagreement about what produced the midterm Democratic wave.

Brookings scholars Elaine Kamarck and William Galston argue that Republican abstention – those who chose not to vote – was more important nationally than large-scale partisan crossover voting. They report that only approximately 6% of self-identified Republicans voted for Democratic House candidates.

Yet the evidence also demonstrates some crossover voting.

An analysis by the research firm NORC found that approximately 1 in 10 2024 Trump voters in 2026 supported Democratic Senate candidates in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina and Texas.

Both dynamics appear to have played a role. 

Democrats benefited from stronger participation among their supporters and reduced turnout among some voters who backed Trump in 2024. In several competitive races, Republican defections and strong independent support also contributed to Democratic victories.

Understanding these differences is important. A shift in election results does not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. It may reflect changes in who participates. The 2026 results suggest that both factors were at work.

Younger voters shifted sharply toward Democrats

Gen Z voters were another important part of the Democratic gains.

In 2026, 66% of voters ages 18–29 supported Democratic House candidates, compared with 30% who backed Republicans. That 36-point Democratic advantage was substantially larger than the 14-point margin in 2024, according to Tufts University.

There was also evidence of voters switching party choices. Among young people who voted for Trump in 2024 and participated in the 2026 election, 16% supported a Democratic House candidate. And 67% of young voters disapproved of Trump’s performance as president in 2026.

Gallup found that 56% of Gen Z adults identify as political independents, underscoring the weaker ties many younger Americans have to the two major parties. 

Combined with economic dissatisfaction and distrust of political institutions, this suggests that younger voters may be especially willing to reconsider their choices when the party in power fails to meet their expectations or deliver on its promises.

Latino voters also shifted substantially

Latino voters showed a similar pattern, but with some differences.

More than 6 in 10 Latino voters supported Democratic House candidates in 2026, according to a NORC survey. That reverses much of the Republican gains among these voters in 2024.

There was also evidence of volatility among Latinos. A postelection survey by UnidosUS and BSP Research found that 17% of Latino voters who supported Trump in 2024 voted for Democratic House candidates in 2026, compared with just 3% of Harris voters who supported Republicans.

Texas offers an example of how these voting groups overlapped.

According to our analysis of the voter poll data, 68% of Latino voters supported Democrat James Talarico, compared with 30% who backed his Republican opponent. Among voters ages 18 to 29, Talarico won 79% to 19%, while independents favored him by 64% to 33%.

Of course, these groups overlap. A voter can be Latino, young and independent, so their contributions cannot simply be added together numerically.

Still, Latinos’ strong support for Talarico illustrates how shifts among these voting groups helped Democrats win in a traditionally Republican state, perhaps shaping a new composite demographic.

A warning for both political parties

The lesson of 2026 may be less about Democratic realignment than about political accountability.

Republicans benefited in 2024 from dissatisfaction with Democratic governance. Two years later, Democrats benefited from dissatisfaction with Republican governance.

Yet the scale of the Democratic victories should not be understated. 

Widespread dissatisfaction with Trump’s presidency – his handling of the economy, the war in Iran, harsh immigration enforcement policies and concerns about corruption – contributed to a sweeping rejection of his administration and Republican leadership at both the federal and state levels. That includes a Congress that many voters believed had failed to hold him accountable.

Even so, neither party should assume that independents, younger voters or Latinos now belong to its camp.

America’s founders recognized the dangers of excessive party loyalty. In his 1796 farewell address, George Washington warned about the divisive influence of political parties and the dangers of placing party allegiance above the public interest.

More than two centuries later, the growing influence of voters with weaker ties to the major parties raises a similar question about the role of political parties in American democracy.

The 2026 election may not signal a lasting political realignment. Instead, it may reflect an electorate increasingly willing to hold both parties accountable.

For Democrats and Republicans alike, winning an election does not necessarily mean winning voters’ lasting loyalty.
news.summary: Midterm election results do not necessarily mean voters have changed their party loyalties. Instead, it may reflect an electorate increasingly willing to hold both parties accountable.
